items.caption: Figure 1: Overall pre-training and fine-tuning procedures for BERT. Apart from output layers, the same architec- tures are used in both pre-training and fine-tuning. The same pre-trained model parameters are used to initialize models for different down-stream tasks. During fine-tuning, all parameters are fine-tuned. [CLS] is a special symbol added in front of every input example, and [SEP] is a special separator token (e.g. separating ques- tions/answers).
items.title: The Same Stack, Twice
items.takeaway: The figure claims that pre-training and fine-tuning use one and the same network: an identical token-in, vector-out Transformer encoder appears in both panels, and the only thing that changes between them is the thin output layer bolted on top. The dotted arrows carry every pre-trained weight across to initialize the task model, so a downstream task inherits the whole network rather than a set of embeddings.
items.walkthrough:
You are looking at one block diagram drawn twice. The left panel shows [[bert]] being pre-trained; the right shows the same stack being fine-tuned on an end task. The visual argument is that the two boxes are drawn identically on purpose.

Read each panel bottom to top.

At the bottom, pink boxes hold the raw input: `[CLS]`, `Tok 1 … Tok N`, `[SEP]`, then `Tok 1 … Tok M`. Two spans of text are packed into a single sequence ([[sentence-pair-packing]]), labelled Sentence A and Sentence B. A "sentence" here is any contiguous run of text, not a grammatical one ([[sentence-as-arbitrary-span]]).

Two of those tokens are special. [[cls-token]] is prepended to every input, and its output vector is what classification heads read. [[sep-token]] marks the boundary between A and B.

The yellow row above is the input embeddings, written $E_{[CLS]}, E_1 \dots E_N, E_{[SEP]}, E'_1 \dots E'_M$. A prime means the token came from Sentence B. Each $E$ is a sum of token, segment and [[position-embeddings]] ([[input-embedding-sum]]).

The blue slab labelled BERT is a multi-layer [[transformer-encoder]]. The threads inside it fan from every position to every other, standing for [[bidirectional-self-attention]] — each layer sees left and right context at once.

Out of the top come green boxes: $C$ at the `[CLS]` position ([[final-hidden-vector-c]]) and $T_1 \dots T'_M$ elsewhere ([[final-hidden-vector-ti]]). These are just final hidden vectors, one per input token.

Now the red arrows on top. This is the only place the two panels differ.

On the left there are two heads. [[masked-language-model]] sits over token outputs and predicts the original identity of tokens that were hidden — hence "Masked Sentence A/B". [[next-sentence-prediction]] sits over $C$ alone and predicts whether B really followed A. The blue arrow underneath says the pair is unlabeled: both training signals come from raw text ([[unlabeled-text]]).

Between the panels, the dotted arrows are parameter transfer. Every weight learned on the left initializes the stack on the right. Nothing else crosses.

The right panel stacks three cards — [[mnli]], [[conll-2003-ner]], [[squad-v1-1]] — one per task. Only the head is new ([[task-specific-output-layer]]): MNLI reads $C$, NER reads each $T_i$, SQuAD's Start/End Span head scores each passage token as a span boundary ([[span-prediction-head]]).

Then everything, not just the head, is trained ([[end-to-end-fine-tuning]]). Each task therefore ends up with its own separate copy ([[separate-fine-tuned-models-per-task]]).

terms.definition: The label on the left panel: the stage where BERT is trained on plain unlabeled text using objectives that need no human annotation. It is run once, and its output is a set of weights.
The label on the right panel: the stage where the pre-trained weights are loaded and then trained further on a labeled end task. It is run once per task.

The shared body of the model, a multi-layer bidirectional Transformer encoder. It maps a sequence of input embeddings to a sequence of contextual output vectors, and is the part that appears unchanged in both panels.

terms.term: The threads drawn inside the slab
terms.definition: A schematic of self-attention layers: each node connects to all positions, not only to positions on its left. This is the picture of bidirectional conditioning that the paper contrasts with left-to-right models.
A special token added in front of every input sequence. Its final hidden vector is used as the aggregate representation of the whole sequence for classification.
A special separator token placed between Sentence A and Sentence B, and at the end of the sequence. It tells the model where one packed span ends and the next begins.
The WordPiece tokens of Sentence A, shown as pink boxes at the bottom left of each panel. They are sub-word units drawn from a fixed 30,000-entry vocabulary, not whole words.
The WordPiece tokens of Sentence B, the second packed span. The counts N and M are independent, so the two spans may have different lengths.

terms.term: Masked Sentence A / Masked Sentence B
terms.definition: The bracket labels under the pink token rows in the left panel. They mark that during pre-training some of these input tokens have been corrupted before being fed in.

terms.term: Unlabeled Sentence A and B Pair
terms.definition: The caption on the blue input arrow in the left panel. It states that the pre-training example carries no human annotation: both training targets are derived from the text itself.

An input embedding for one token position, the vector actually fed into the first Transformer layer. Each E is the sum of a token embedding, a segment embedding saying A or B, and a position embedding.
The input embeddings of the two special tokens. They are ordinary learned embeddings; nothing about the special tokens is hard-coded at the input side.
A notational tag meaning the position belongs to Sentence B rather than Sentence A. It is bookkeeping in the diagram, not a different kind of vector.
The final hidden vector at the [CLS] position, in R^H. It is the vector that sequence-level heads read; the paper notes it is not a meaningful sentence representation until it has been fine-tuned.
The final hidden vector for the i-th input token, in R^H. There is exactly one per input position, and token-level heads read these.
The output vector sitting above the separator token. It exists because every position produces an output, though no head in this figure uses it.
The pre-training head over token outputs: a softmax over the vocabulary that predicts the original identity of tokens that were hidden in the input. Only the chosen positions contribute loss.

Next Sentence Prediction, the pre-training head over C: a binary classifier deciding whether Sentence B is the text that actually followed Sentence A in the corpus. It is drawn over C alone, not over the token outputs.

terms.term: The dotted arrows between the panels
terms.definition: Parameter transfer: all pre-trained weights are copied over to initialize the downstream model. The paper stresses that everything transfers, not only an embedding table.

terms.term: The stacked cards in the right panel
terms.definition: Three overlapping copies of the same diagram, one per downstream task. They depict separate fine-tuned models that all start from the same pre-trained parameters.
Multi-Genre Natural Language Inference: given a sentence pair, label it entailment, contradiction, or neutral. It is a sequence-level task, so its head reads C.
Named Entity Recognition, evaluated on CoNLL-2003 here: label each token with an entity type. It is a token-level task, so its head reads each T_i independently.
The Stanford Question Answering Dataset: given a question and a Wikipedia paragraph, mark the span of the paragraph that answers it. It is the running example the section text follows.
The SQuAD output head. Two learned vectors S and E score every passage token as a possible span start and span end, each through a softmax over passage positions.
The bracket labels in the right panel replacing Sentence A and Sentence B. The question is packed as segment A and the passage as segment B, in one sequence.
The caption on the blue input arrow in the right panel. Unlike the left panel's input, this example is labeled: the correct answer span is known during fine-tuning.
Output heads, drawn above the green output boxes. They are the only components that differ between the two panels and the only parameters learned from scratch per task.
Elisions standing for the remaining token positions in each span. They indicate that N and M are arbitrary, not that positions are missing.
The two spans packed into one input sequence. Throughout the paper a 'sentence' is any contiguous span of text, so these may be a question and a paragraph, or a premise and a hypothesis.

numbers.meaning: The number of panels. The figure is deliberately drawn as two copies of one diagram, which is the visual form of the paper's claim that there is minimal difference between the pre-trained architecture and the downstream architecture.

The number of stacked task cards on the right (MNLI, NER, SQuAD). It is illustrative, not exhaustive: the paper fine-tunes on eleven tasks in total, and the three shown are chosen to span a sequence-level task, a token-level tagging task, and a span-prediction task.
The number of tokens in Sentence A, shown as the subscript on the last A-side box (Tok N, E_N, T_N). It is a placeholder, since spans vary in length.
The number of tokens in Sentence B, shown as the primed subscript (Tok M, E'_M, T'_M). It is independent of N, which is why the diagram gives it a separate letter.
The starting index in each span (Tok 1, E_1, T_1, and their primed counterparts). Indexing restarts at 1 after [SEP] because the primes already distinguish segment B.

The share of WordPiece token positions chosen at random for masked prediction in each sequence. It sets how many of the green boxes actually feed a Mask LM arrow: the figure draws two such arrows, but in practice roughly one position in seven is predicted.

Of the chosen 15% of positions, 80% are replaced with the [MASK] token, 10% with a random token, and 10% are left unchanged. The paper's reason is that [MASK] never appears at fine-tuning time, so always inserting it would create a mismatch between the two panels.

The class balance of the NSP head's training data: half the time Sentence B is the real continuation of A (IsNext), half the time it is a random sentence from the corpus (NotNext). The even split makes chance accuracy 50%, so the reported 97-98% NSP accuracy is above a clear floor.
The hidden size, the dimension of every C and T_i box in the figure: C and T_i are both in R^H. It is 768 for BERT_BASE and 1024 for BERT_LARGE, so the same diagram describes both model sizes.
The number of Transformer layers stacked inside the blue slab: 12 for BERT_BASE, 24 for BERT_LARGE. The figure draws only a few rows of nodes, so the depth shown is schematic.

Total parameter counts for BERT_BASE and BERT_LARGE. These are the quantities the dotted arrows transfer; the task heads added on the right add only a few thousand parameters by comparison, which is the paper's point about minimal task-specific parameters.
The size of the WordPiece vocabulary the pink token boxes are drawn from, and hence the width of the Mask LM output softmax.

items.caption: Figure 2: BERT input representation. The input embeddings are the sum of the token embeddings, the segmenta- tion embeddings and the position embeddings.
items.title: The Three-Row Input Sum
items.takeaway: Every token BERT reads is a single vector formed by adding three learned vectors together: what the token is, which of the two packed spans it belongs to, and where it sits in the sequence. This one format carries both single texts and text pairs, so the same encoder serves every task without changing its input plumbing.
items.walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

A worked example of BERT's [[input-representation]], for the eleven-token sequence `[CLS] my dog is cute [SEP] he likes play ##ing [SEP]`.

There are four rows. The top row is the tokens themselves. The three rows below it are vectors, and the `+` signs stacked between them say those three are added together.

### How to read it

Read one column at a time. Each column is a single position in the sequence, and its three coloured boxes are the three vectors that make that position's input.

The top row shows what the tokenizer produced. Two special tokens appear: [[cls-token]], always first, and [[sep-token]], which closes each span. The word *playing* has been split by [[wordpiece-tokenization]] into `play` and `##ing`; the `##` prefix marks a piece that continues the previous one rather than starting a new word.

The **Token Embeddings** row is the ordinary lookup: $E_{\text{my}}$ is the vector stored for the vocabulary entry *my*. The two `[SEP]` columns share one vector, $E_{\text{[SEP]}}$, because they are the same vocabulary item.

The **Segment Embeddings** row is where [[sentence-pair-packing]] shows up. There are only two possible values here. Columns 0 through 5 get $E_A$, columns 6 through 10 get $E_B$. Note that the first `[SEP]` takes $E_A$ — the boundary marker is counted as part of the span it closes. These are [[segment-embeddings]]: a learned tag saying *first span* or *second span*.

The **Position Embeddings** row runs $E_0$ through $E_{10}$, one distinct vector per slot. These [[position-embeddings]] are the only thing telling the model about order, since self-attention itself sees the sequence as a set.

### What it shows

The sum is elementwise, per column. Position 8's input is $E_{\text{play}} + E_B + E_8$, a single vector of the model's hidden width — not a concatenation, so the three signals share the same dimensions and the width never grows. That vector is what enters layer one.

This is the [[input-embedding-sum]], and it is the whole of BERT's input encoding.

terms.definition: The top row's label. It names the token sequence after tokenization — what BERT actually indexes, rather than the raw text the user supplied.

A special token placed first in every sequence. Its final hidden state is used as the aggregate representation of the whole input for classification tasks; here it simply occupies position 0 and gets the same three-way sum as any other token.
A special token marking a span boundary. It appears twice here: once closing the first span and once closing the sequence. Both instances share the same token embedding.
A WordPiece continuation piece. The `##` prefix means this piece attaches to the preceding piece rather than beginning a new word, so `play` + `##ing` reconstructs *playing*.
The subword tokenizer used here, with a 30,000-token vocabulary. Words outside the vocabulary are broken into known pieces, which is why *playing* becomes two columns in the figure.
The second row: a plain lookup table from vocabulary entry to vector. This row carries what the token is, with no information about position or which span it came from.

terms.term: E_[CLS], E_my, E_dog, E_is, E_cute, E_he, E_likes, E_play, E_##ing, E_[SEP]
terms.definition: Individual entries of that lookup table, one per vocabulary item present in the example. Identical tokens anywhere in any sequence get the identical vector from this row.
The third row: a learned vector added to every token indicating whether it belongs to span A or span B. It is what lets one sequence unambiguously hold a pair of texts.
The segment vector for the first packed span. In this example it is added at positions 0 through 5, covering `[CLS] my dog is cute [SEP]`.
The segment vector for the second packed span. Here it is added at positions 6 through 10, covering `he likes play ##ing [SEP]`.
The paper's names for the two spans packed into one sequence. A "sentence" here means any span of contiguous text, not a linguistic sentence.
The bottom row: one learned vector per slot in the sequence. Self-attention has no built-in notion of order, so this row is what carries it.
The eleven distinct position vectors used by this example, indexed from 0. The subscript is the slot number, not anything about the token that lands there.
The stacked plus signs between rows. They denote elementwise addition of the three vectors within a column, producing one vector per position.
The paper's notation for the resulting per-token input vector — the sum of that token's token, segment and position embeddings. It is the vector fed into the first Transformer layer.
The model whose input format this figure specifies: a multi-layer bidirectional Transformer encoder, pre-trained on unlabeled text and then fine-tuned per task.

numbers.meaning: Rows in the figure. One is the token sequence itself; the other three are the embedding tables whose outputs are summed. The count is a design fact, not a tuned value — the paper names exactly three signals a token needs: identity, span membership, and position.

Columns, i.e. tokens in the example sequence. It is what `[CLS] my dog is cute [SEP] he likes play ##ing [SEP]` comes to after tokenization: 4 content words plus [CLS] and [SEP] in span A, and 3 content pieces plus [SEP] in span B. The value is incidental to the example.
Positions carrying E_A (indices 0–5). Span A is `[CLS] my dog is cute [SEP]` — four words, the leading [CLS], and the closing [SEP], which is tagged A rather than B.
Positions carrying E_B (indices 6–10): `he likes play ##ing [SEP]`. Four pieces plus the final separator.
Distinct segment embeddings in existence, E_A and E_B. The input format supports at most two packed spans, so the segment table has exactly two rows regardless of sequence length.

Occurrences of [SEP] in the example: one at index 5 closing span A, one at index 10 closing the sequence. Both draw the same token embedding, and are told apart only by their segment and position vectors.
The first position index. Numbering starts at 0, so E_0 sits under [CLS] and the last of eleven tokens is E_10, not E_11.
The range of position-embedding subscripts shown. Each index has its own learned vector; the figure shows only as many as this example needs.

Size of the WordPiece vocabulary (from Section 3, not printed in the figure). It is the number of rows in the Token Embeddings table, and the reason rare words like *playing* get split into pieces that are in the table.

The maximum sequence length BERT is trained with (Section A.2). It bounds how far the position-embedding subscripts can run, so the position table has 512 rows even though this example uses 11 of them. Appendix A.2 says the last 10% of pre-training steps use length-512 sequences specifically so the longer-range position embeddings get trained.

The hidden size H for BERT_BASE and BERT_LARGE (Section 3). Every box in all three embedding rows is a vector of this width — that is what makes elementwise addition possible, and why the summed input is the same width as a single row rather than three times it.

items.caption: Table 1: GLUE Test results, scored by the evaluation server (https://gluebenchmark.com/leaderboard). The number below each task denotes the number of training examples. The “Average” column is slightly different than the official GLUE score, since we exclude the problematic WNLI set.8 BERT and OpenAI GPT are single- model, single task. F1 scores are reported for QQP and MRPC, Spearman correlations are reported for STS-B, and accuracy scores are reported for the other tasks. We exclude entries that use BERT as one of their components.
items.title: The GLUE test scoreboard
items.takeaway: On the eight scored GLUE tasks, both BERT sizes beat every prior system in every column, lifting the average by 4.5 points (BERT_BASE) and 7.0 points (BERT_LARGE) over OpenAI GPT, with a 4.6-point gain on MNLI. Because BERT_BASE is the same size as GPT, the paper reads the gap as evidence for bidirectional pre-training rather than for extra capacity.
items.walkthrough:
You are looking at a scoreboard. Five systems run down the left, eight scored task columns run across, and one averaged column closes the table. Every number is a score on the test split of a dataset in the [[glue-benchmark]], a bundle of English sentence and sentence-pair classification tasks under one submission format.

Read the header block first. The top header row names the task. The row underneath gives that task's training-set size, from 392k examples for [[mnli]] down to 2.5k for [[rte]]. The Average column has a dash there, because an average is not a dataset.

None of these numbers were scored locally. GLUE withholds test labels, so authors submit predictions and the [[glue-evaluation-server]] returns the score.

The metric changes from column to column. The caption reports [[f1-score]] for [[qqp]] and [[mrpc]], Spearman rank correlation for [[sts-b]] — whose labels are a graded 1-to-5 similarity, not a class — and accuracy for the rest. MNLI carries two numbers split by a slash: matched, where test genres also appear in training, and mismatched, where they do not.

Now the rows. Pre-OpenAI SOTA takes the best published number per column from before [[openai-gpt]], so different columns may come from different systems. BiLSTM+ELMo+Attn is GLUE's own baseline: a [[bilstm]] task model with attention, fed features from [[elmo]]. Then GPT, then [[bert-base-and-bert-large]], with the best number in each column set in bold.

What the table shows is a clean sweep. Both BERT rows sit above every earlier row in every column.

Walk the average. GPT holds the prior best at 75.1. BERT_BASE reaches 79.6, which is 4.5 points higher. BERT_LARGE reaches 82.1, which is 7.0 points higher. On MNLI, the largest of these sets, 86.7 against GPT's 82.1 is the 4.6-point gain the abstract quotes.

BERT_BASE was sized to match GPT ([[gpt-size-match]]), so that row-to-row gap is the paper's main evidence that bidirectionality, not scale, is doing the work.

Three limits are stated in the caption. [[wnli]] is dropped from the Average. Every entry is one model fine-tuned on one task ([[single-task-vs-multi-task-fine-tuning]]). Systems that already contain BERT are excluded from the comparison.

terms.definition: The left-hand column, naming the model whose scores fill that row. Rows are ordered roughly by publication, oldest at the top.

The General Language Understanding Evaluation benchmark: a collection of separate natural-language-understanding datasets gathered under one submission format and leaderboard. This table reports each of its tasks as its own column.
The word in the caption signalling that these are held-out test-split scores, not development-set scores. GLUE does not release test labels.
The GLUE service that scores a submitted prediction file against the hidden test labels and returns a number. Every cell in this table came back from it.
Multi-Genre Natural Language Inference: given a premise and a hypothesis, label the pair entailment, contradiction or neutral. The two scores are the matched and mismatched test sets.
The MNLI test half whose text genres also appear in the training data, so it measures in-domain accuracy.
The MNLI test half drawn from genres absent from training, so it measures out-of-domain accuracy. It is consistently the lower of the two numbers here.
Quora Question Pairs: decide whether two questions posted on Quora ask the same thing. Scored by F1 because the two classes are unbalanced.

Question Natural Language Inference: SQuAD recast as a binary decision on whether a given sentence contains the answer to a given question. Negatives are sentences from the same paragraph that do not.
The Stanford Sentiment Treebank, binary form: label a single sentence pulled from a movie review as positive or negative.
The Corpus of Linguistic Acceptability: judge whether a single English sentence is linguistically acceptable. Its scores sit far below every other column, so read it on its own scale.

The Semantic Textual Similarity Benchmark: sentence pairs from news headlines and elsewhere, annotated with a 1-to-5 similarity rating. Because the label is a graded score rather than a class, it is scored by correlation.
Microsoft Research Paraphrase Corpus: sentence pairs harvested from online news, labelled by humans for whether the two sentences mean the same thing.
Recognizing Textual Entailment: a binary entailment decision, the same shape of task as MNLI but with roughly 150 times less training data.
The mean of the eight task scores in that row, with MNLI's matched and mismatched numbers counting as one task. The caption flags that this differs slightly from the official GLUE score.

Winograd NLI, the ninth GLUE task, absent from this table. The paper drops it because the GLUE authors themselves note construction problems, and every submitted system scores below the majority-class floor.
The best published result on each task from before OpenAI GPT. It is a per-column high-water mark, so different cells in this row can come from different systems.
The GLUE paper's own baseline: a bidirectional LSTM task model with attention, taking ELMo's contextual word features as input. It stands in for the feature-based transfer approach.
A recurrent layer run left-to-right and right-to-left over the sequence, with the two directions joined at each position. Here it is the task-specific model sitting on top of frozen ELMo features.
An attention layer between the two sentences in the GLUE baseline model, letting each token of one sentence weigh tokens of the other.
A left-to-right Transformer language model, pre-trained then fine-tuned per task. It is the immediately prior state of the art and the row BERT's gains are measured against.
The 12-layer, 768-hidden, 12-head configuration, 110M parameters, deliberately sized to equal OpenAI GPT so the comparison isolates bidirectional pre-training from capacity.
The 24-layer, 1024-hidden, 16-head configuration, 340M parameters. It holds the bold best score in every column of this table.
The two reported BERT configurations differ only in depth, width and head count; both use the same pre-training data and objectives.
The harmonic mean of precision and recall, used here for QQP and MRPC, where one class dominates and plain accuracy would flatter a lazy classifier.

A rank correlation between predicted and human similarity scores, used for STS-B because its labels are ordered ratings rather than categories. A value of 100 would mean the model ranks all pairs exactly as the annotators did.
The fraction of test examples labelled correctly, the metric the caption assigns to MNLI, QNLI, SST-2, CoLA and RTE.
The caption's statement that each BERT and GPT number comes from one model fine-tuned on that one task, with no ensembling and no multi-task training.
Thousands of labelled training examples available for that task. It is the second header row, not a score.
Marks the best value in each column. Every bold cell falls in the BERT_LARGE row.

numbers.meaning: The training-set sizes under each column header, in order: MNLI 392k, QQP 363k, QNLI 108k, SST-2 67k, CoLA 8.5k, STS-B 5.7k, MRPC 3.5k, RTE 2.5k. They span more than two orders of magnitude, which is why the paper reads BERT's biggest wins on the right-hand, low-data columns as a statement about small datasets.
The dash under the Average header. Average is a computed column, not a dataset, so it has no training set.

The Pre-OpenAI SOTA row: the best published score per task before GPT. Because each cell can come from a different system, this row is a composite ceiling rather than one model, which is why GPT beats it on some columns (MNLI, QQP, QNLI, CoLA) but not others (SST-2 93.2 vs 91.3, STS-B 81.0 vs 80.0, MRPC 86.0 vs 82.3, RTE 61.7 vs 56.0).
The BiLSTM+ELMo+Attn row, GLUE's feature-based baseline. It is the lowest average in the table at 71.0, and it trails the pre-GPT per-task ceiling on every column except CoLA (36.0 against 35.0).
The OpenAI GPT row and the baseline BERT's gains are quoted against. Its 75.1 average is the prior state of the art, and its CoLA jump to 45.4 from 35.0 is its largest single-column gain.

The BERT_BASE row. Every cell is above the corresponding GPT cell and above both earlier rows, which matters because BERT_BASE and GPT have the same parameter count and nearly the same architecture apart from attention masking.

The BERT_LARGE row, bold in every column because it is the best value everywhere. It beats BERT_BASE on all eight tasks, which the paper points at as motivation for the model-size study in Section 5.2.
BERT_BASE's average gain over the prior state of the art: 79.6 minus GPT's 75.1. It is the headline number for the size-matched comparison.
BERT_LARGE's average gain: 82.1 minus 75.1. The extra 2.5 points over BERT_BASE's gain come from scaling the model, not from a different objective.
The MNLI-matched gain the paper quotes: BERT_LARGE's 86.7 minus GPT's 82.1. MNLI is singled out as the largest and most widely reported GLUE task, so it carries the most weight.

The CoLA column top to bottom. Every value sits far below every other column, so CoLA drags each row's average down; BERT_LARGE's 60.5 is 15.1 points above GPT, the widest single-column margin in the table.

RTE for GPT, BERT_BASE and BERT_LARGE. On the smallest training set in the table, 2.5k examples, BERT_BASE gains 10.4 points and BERT_LARGE 14.1, which is the pattern the paper describes as larger models helping most where data is scarce.
MRPC F1 for GPT, BERT_BASE and BERT_LARGE. GPT sits below the 86.0 pre-GPT ceiling here, so BERT's 89.3 is the first entry in this column to clear the older result.
SST-2 accuracy for Pre-OpenAI SOTA, BERT_BASE and BERT_LARGE. The margin is under two points, the narrowest in the table, because the task was already close to saturated.

Quoted in the surrounding text, not in the table: BERT_LARGE's and OpenAI GPT's official GLUE leaderboard scores at the time of writing. These include WNLI, which the table's Average excludes, so they do not match the 82.1 and 75.1 shown here.
The abstract's stated absolute improvement in the official GLUE score, 80.5 minus 72.8. It is larger than the table's 7.0 because the official score is computed over a different set of tasks.

The WNLI majority-class baseline accuracy mentioned in Appendix B.1. No submitted system had beaten it, which is the paper's stated reason for excluding WNLI from the Average and for simply predicting the majority class on it.
The table scores eight tasks; GLUE has nine. The missing one is WNLI, dropped for fairness to OpenAI GPT as well as for the dataset's known problems.

From the surrounding text: every GLUE fine-tuning run used batch size 32 for 3 epochs, with only the learning rate chosen per task from {5e-5, 4e-5, 3e-5, 2e-5} on the development set. The uniformity is part of the claim that no per-task architecture work was needed.

items.caption: Table 2: SQuAD 1.1 results. The BERT ensemble is 7x systems which use different pre-training check- points and fine-tuning seeds.
items.title: BERT against the SQuAD leaderboard
items.takeaway: On SQuAD 1.1 span extraction, a fine-tuned BERT_LARGE ensemble reaches 93.2 test F1 and a single fine-tuned BERT_LARGE reaches 91.8, which the paper reports as +1.5 F1 and +1.3 F1 over the top leaderboard system of the day. Both figures come with an asterisk the paper states itself: the leaderboard entries may train on any public data, so BERT is first fine-tuned on TriviaQA to match, and dropping that extra data costs only 0.1-0.4 points.
items.walkthrough:
This is a scoreboard for a single task: answering a question by marking the [[answer-span]] inside a Wikipedia passage, measured on [[squad-v1-1]]. Rows are systems, columns are scores, higher is better.

### Reading the columns

The four score columns are two splits crossed with two metrics. **Dev** is the public development set ([[dev-set-model-selection]]), which anyone can score locally. **Test** labels are held by the benchmark organisers, so a Test number exists only for systems actually submitted for scoring.

Inside each split sit **EM** and **F1** ([[exact-match-and-f1]]). EM is the percentage of questions where the predicted string matches a human answer exactly. [[f1-score]] instead treats prediction and answer as bags of tokens and takes the harmonic mean of precision and recall.

So a prediction that catches the right words but runs one word long earns most of an F1 point and zero EM. That is why F1 exceeds EM in every row printed here.

A dash means "not reported", and the dashes fall in a pattern. Leaderboard rows carry Test only; BERT rows without TriviaQA carry Dev only.

### Reading the groups

**Top Leaderboard Systems (Dec 10th, 2018)** is the live leaderboard at the time of writing, plus a **Human** row for human agreement. The paper notes these entries have no up-to-date public system descriptions and may train on any public data ([[squad-leaderboard-public-data-rules]]).

**Published** holds systems with papers behind them ([[prior-squad-systems]]), both purpose-built reading-comprehension architectures.

**Ours** is BERT ([[bert]]), which adds only a start and an end vector on top of the pre-trained encoder ([[span-prediction-head]]).

### What it shows

BERT_BASE reaches 88.5 dev F1; BERT_LARGE reaches 90.9 ([[bert-base-and-bert-large]]). [[ensembling]] seven systems — different pre-training checkpoints and fine-tuning seeds — adds another 0.9 to 91.8 dev.

Adding [[triviaqa-augmentation]] before SQuAD fine-tuning gives the two submitted rows. The ensemble's 93.2 test F1 sits 1.5 above nlnet's 91.7, which is the headline margin ([[absolute-improvement]]) and is the one figure you can read straight off the table.

The single-system +1.3 is not reproducible from these cells: against nlnet's 91.7, the single BERT's 91.8 is +0.1, which is the separate claim the paper makes next — a single BERT beating the top ensemble on F1.

terms.definition: The first column, naming the model or entry that produced the row's scores. Entries are grouped into three blocks separated by horizontal rules.

The Stanford Question Answering Dataset, version 1.1: roughly 100k crowdsourced question/answer pairs where the answer is always a contiguous span of an accompanying Wikipedia passage. Every number in this table is measured on it.
The public development split, whose labels are distributed with the dataset. Anyone can score on it without submitting anything, which is why the paper reports its own unsubmitted variants here.
The held-out split whose labels the benchmark organisers keep private. A number appears here only if the system was submitted to them for official evaluation.

The percentage of questions where the predicted span string exactly matches a human-provided answer, after light normalisation of punctuation, articles and whitespace. It is all-or-nothing per question.

Token-overlap credit: the predicted span and the gold answer are treated as bags of tokens, and the score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall between them, averaged over questions. It gives partial credit where EM gives none, so it is always the higher of the two here.

The first row group: the highest-scoring entries on the public SQuAD leaderboard on the date the paper was written. The paper notes these entries lack up-to-date public descriptions and are allowed to train on any public data.
A human-performance row from the dataset's own paper, obtained by scoring one person's answers against the other human answers for the same questions. It is a reference line, not a competing system.
The top-ranked leaderboard entry at the cutoff date, itself an ensemble. This is the system the paper's headline ensemble margin is measured against.

The second-ranked leaderboard entry, an ensemble of the QANet architecture (Yu et al., 2018). The paper footnotes that the leaderboard version has improved substantially beyond the published description.
The second row group: systems whose descriptions exist in the literature, so their training data and architecture are known. A fairer but weaker comparison set than the leaderboard block.
Bidirectional Attention Flow (Seo et al., 2017), a purpose-built reading-comprehension network, with ELMo contextual embeddings fed in as extra input features.
The Reinforced Mnemonic Reader (Hu et al., 2018), an ensemble; the strongest published system in the table before BERT.
The third row group: the paper's own five BERT configurations, all fine-tuned from the same pre-trained encoders.
The smaller pre-trained configuration, 12 layers with hidden size 768 and 12 attention heads, about 110M parameters.
The larger pre-trained configuration, 24 layers with hidden size 1024 and 16 attention heads, about 340M parameters.
One fine-tuned model producing the predictions, with no combination across runs.

Predictions combined across several fine-tuned models. For BERT, the caption specifies 7x systems that differ in which pre-training checkpoint they started from and which fine-tuning random seed they used.
A single BERT_LARGE fine-tuned first on TriviaQA and then on SQuAD. The paper calls this modest data augmentation, adopted because leaderboard systems may use any public data.
The seven-model BERT_LARGE ensemble where each member was fine-tuned on TriviaQA before SQuAD. This is the paper's best-performing system.
A separate large reading-comprehension dataset (Joshi et al., 2017), used here only as an intermediate fine-tuning stage before SQuAD, never as an evaluation target.

Not reported. Leaderboard rows show no Dev because the leaderboard publishes Test only; the three BERT rows without TriviaQA show no Test because those variants were not submitted for official scoring.
Marks the two submitted +TriviaQA rows, the systems the paper puts forward as its results rather than as internal comparisons.
A saved snapshot of the pre-trained encoder's weights. Ensemble members start from different snapshots, so they differ before any task data is seen.
The random seed governing fine-tuning: initialisation of the new output vectors, data shuffling and dropout. Varying it makes ensemble members differ even from the same checkpoint.
The only task-specific parameters BERT adds for SQuAD: a start vector S and an end vector E, each of hidden size H, dotted with every token's final vector to score it as a span start or end.

numbers.meaning: The approximate number of crowdsourced question/answer pairs in SQuAD v1.1, from which the Dev and Test splits are drawn. The paper cites it to place SQuAD among the larger labeled datasets it fine-tunes on.
The date the leaderboard snapshot in the first row group was taken. It is printed because the leaderboard is live and the top entries move, so the comparison is only valid as of that day.

Human Test EM and F1. The gap between them says humans often phrase the answer with slightly different boundaries than the reference answer, which EM punishes and F1 does not. Both BERT +TriviaQA rows exceed both figures on Test.
nlnet's Test EM and F1 as the #1 leaderboard entry. The 91.7 F1 is the reference point for the paper's +1.5 ensemble margin.
QANet's Test EM and F1 as the #2 leaderboard entry, 1.2 F1 behind nlnet.
BiDAF+ELMo Dev F1 and Test F1. Its EM cells are dashed, so only F1 is available; the near-identical Dev and Test values suggest the two splits are of comparable difficulty.
R.M. Reader Dev EM and F1, the strongest published Dev numbers in the table before BERT.
R.M. Reader Test EM and F1. Its 88.5 Test F1 is the published state of the art BERT is measured against; its 82.3 Test EM coincidentally equals the human EM figure.
BERT_BASE single Dev EM and F1. Its Dev F1 already matches the best published Test F1 in the table, from a 110M-parameter encoder with only two extra task vectors.
BERT_LARGE single Dev EM and F1. The 2.4 F1 gain over BERT_BASE comes from model size alone, since both use the same fine-tuning recipe.
BERT_LARGE ensemble Dev EM and F1, without TriviaQA. Ensembling seven fine-tuning runs adds 0.9 F1 and 1.7 EM over the single model.
BERT_LARGE single +TriviaQA Dev EM and F1. Compared with 84.1 / 90.9 without TriviaQA, the intermediate fine-tuning is worth 0.1 EM and 0.2 F1 on Dev.

BERT_LARGE single +TriviaQA Test EM and F1. The 91.8 F1 is the single-system headline; it exceeds nlnet's 91.7 ensemble by 0.1, which is the paper's claim that one BERT model beats the top ensemble on F1.
BERT_LARGE ensemble +TriviaQA Dev EM and F1, the best Dev numbers in the table. Against 85.8 / 91.8 without TriviaQA, augmentation is worth 0.4 on both metrics here.
BERT_LARGE ensemble +TriviaQA Test EM and F1, the best result reported. The 93.2 F1 is the number the +1.5 margin is computed from.

The number of models in each BERT ensemble, stated in the caption. They differ in pre-training checkpoint and fine-tuning random seed, so ensemble variance comes from both training stages rather than from architecture changes.
The ensemble margin over the top leaderboard system: 93.2 minus nlnet's 91.7. This one is readable directly from the printed cells.

The single-system margin the paper states. It is not recoverable from the cells shown, since the leaderboard rows here are ensembles and 91.8 minus 91.7 is 0.1; the single-system comparison point is not printed in the table.

What the paper says it loses by dropping TriviaQA fine-tuning. On the Dev cells this is 90.9 vs 91.1 for the single model, a 0.2 gap, and 91.8 vs 92.2 for the ensemble, a 0.4 gap, with the EM differences spanning 0.1 to 0.4.
The SQuAD fine-tuning settings behind every Ours row. They are stated so the results can be read as a short fine-tuning run rather than a heavily tuned one.
Parameter counts of BERT_BASE and BERT_LARGE, the two encoders behind the Ours rows. The 2.4 Dev F1 gap between them is the return on roughly tripling the parameters.

items.caption: Table 3: SQuAD 2.0 results. We exclude entries that use BERT as one of their components.
items.title: SQuAD 2.0 Leaderboard Comparison
items.takeaway: On SQuAD 2.0, where some questions have no answer in the passage, a single fine-tuned BERT_LARGE reaches 83.1 Test F1 against 78.0 for the best prior entry the authors count — a +5.1 F1 gap, on a task the paper handles by adding only two vectors and one threshold. It still sits about 6 F1 below the reported human number, and the comparison is restricted to systems that do not already use BERT inside them.
items.walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

A leaderboard-style results table for [[squad-v2-0]], the version of the Stanford reading-comprehension set that adds [[unanswerable-questions]]: for some question–paragraph pairs the correct output is to abstain rather than to mark a span.

Four number columns, grouped in pairs. The left pair is the development split, the right pair is the held-out test split. Within each pair the two metrics are [[exact-match-and-f1]] — EM scores a prediction only if it matches a gold answer string exactly, while F1 gives partial credit for token overlap. Both are percentages, higher is better.

### How to read it

Rows are grouped by three centred banner labels rather than by an extra column.

*Top Leaderboard Systems (Dec 10th, 2018)* is a snapshot of the public leaderboard on one date; those systems have no full public write-up, so the paper lists them separately from peer-reviewed work. *Published* holds the best described prior systems. *Ours* holds one row.

A dash means the system reports no number for that split. Leaderboard and published entries publish test scores; only BERT reports its own [[dev-set-model-selection]] figures here. The dashes are typeset inconsistently — unet shows two, SLQA+ shows one — but both mean the same absence.

"(Single)" means one model; "(Ensemble)" means several models' predictions combined, which is [[ensembling]] and normally scores higher.

### What it shows

The BERT row is [[bert-base-and-bert-large]] in its 24-layer configuration, fine-tuned as a single model with no [[triviaqa-augmentation]]. It scores 78.7 EM / 81.9 F1 on dev and 80.0 / 83.1 on test.

Subtract: 83.1 minus the 78.0 test F1 of the top leaderboard entry, MIR-MRC (F-Net), gives the +5.1 F1 the paper claims. Note that a single BERT is being compared against an ensemble in the Published block too, and still leads it by 8.2 F1.

Two hedges the table carries. The caption excludes any entry that already uses BERT as a component, so this is not the full leaderboard. And the Human row is above every system: 89.5 test F1, leaving BERT 6.4 F1 short.

The mechanism behind the row is small — abstention is scored as a span at [[cls-as-null-span]], and a single [[tau-threshold]] tuned on dev decides when to answer.

terms.definition: The dataset all rows are scored on: SQuAD v1.1 extended so that a question may have no short answer in the supplied paragraph, which the paper calls a more realistic setting. A system must therefore both find spans and decide when not to answer.
The leftmost column, naming the model or baseline that produced the row's scores. It carries no numbers itself and doubles as the place where the group banners sit.
Column group for the development split, the public set used for tuning hyperparameters and, here, the answering threshold. Scores on it are self-reported and not the headline result.
Column group for the held-out test split, scored by the leaderboard's own evaluation rather than by the authors. These are the numbers the paper's claims rest on.

The fraction of questions where the predicted string matches a gold answer exactly, with an abstention counting as correct only on genuinely unanswerable questions. It is the stricter of the two metrics.
Token-overlap F1 between prediction and gold answer, averaged over questions, giving partial credit when the predicted span is close but not identical. It is always at or above EM on this task.

Banner over the block of public SQuAD 2.0 leaderboard entries as they stood on that date. The paper separates them because such entries have no up-to-date public system description and may train on any public data.
The dataset's own human-performance estimate, obtained by scoring one human annotator's answers against the others. It is a reference ceiling in this table, not a system.
The single model ranked first on the leaderboard snapshot, from an undescribed submission. It is the 'previous best system' the +5.1 F1 claim is measured against.
The second-ranked single-model leaderboard entry, likewise without a public description. It sits just below MIR-MRC on both test metrics.

Banner over the best prior systems that have peer-reviewed descriptions, cited in the text as Sun et al. (2018) and Wang et al. (2018b). Comparing against these is the like-for-like comparison; the leaderboard block is the harder bar.
A published reading-comprehension system, reported as a combination of several models. It is the strongest published entry by test F1 in this table.
A published single-model reading-comprehension system. It ties unet on test EM but trails it slightly on test F1.
Banner over the single row contributed by this paper. Only one BERT configuration is reported for SQuAD 2.0, unlike the SQuAD 1.1 table.
BERT in its 24-layer, 1024-hidden, 16-head configuration (340M parameters), fine-tuned once on SQuAD 2.0 with no ensembling and, unlike the SQuAD 1.1 results, no TriviaQA pre-fine-tuning.
Parenthetical marking a row as one trained model producing predictions on its own. It is the weaker setting and the one BERT is reported in here.

Parenthetical marking a row as several models whose predictions are combined into one answer. It normally buys a point or two over a single model, which is why beating an ensemble with a single model is the sharper comparison.
Placeholder meaning the system reported no score for that cell, here always a Dev number that a leaderboard or published entry did not publish. It does not mean zero or a failure.

terms.term: Entries that use BERT as one of their components
terms.definition: The caption's exclusion: by the time of writing, leaderboard submissions already built on BERT existed, and the authors leave them out so the table compares against non-BERT prior work. This makes the table a filtered view of the leaderboard, not the full ranking.

numbers.meaning: Human Dev EM. The human annotator agrees exactly with the gold answer on 86.3% of development questions, which is why no system row is expected to approach 100.
Human Dev F1. It sits 2.7 points above human EM because partial token overlap earns credit that exact matching does not.
Human Test EM, the human ceiling on the split that all reported system comparisons use.
Human Test F1, the top number in the table. BERT's 83.1 leaves a 6.4 F1 gap, so the paper's improvement does not close the task.
Test EM for #1 MIR-MRC (F-Net), the best exact-match score among non-BERT systems listed.
Test F1 for #1 MIR-MRC (F-Net). This is the 'previous best' baseline: 83.1 minus 78.0 gives the +5.1 F1 improvement stated in Section 4.3 and the abstract.
Test EM for #2 nlnet, 0.6 below the top leaderboard entry.
Test F1 for #2 nlnet, 0.9 below MIR-MRC, showing the two leaderboard leaders were close to each other and far from BERT.
Test EM for both unet (Ensemble) and SLQA+ (Single) — the two published systems tie exactly on this metric, and both sit about 3.4 points below the leaderboard leaders.
Test F1 for unet (Ensemble), the best published (as opposed to leaderboard-only) result here. BERT's 83.1 exceeds it by 8.2 F1, and does so with a single model against an ensemble.
Test F1 for SLQA+ (Single), 0.5 below the unet ensemble despite the identical EM, meaning SLQA+'s near-misses overlap the gold answer slightly less.
BERT_LARGE Dev EM. It is the only Dev EM reported by a system in this table, since the comparison entries publish test numbers only.
BERT_LARGE Dev F1, 3.2 above its Dev EM — the usual EM-to-F1 spread from partially correct spans.
BERT_LARGE Test EM, 1.3 above its own Dev EM. Scoring slightly higher on test than dev is normal split variation, not evidence of tuning on test.
BERT_LARGE Test F1, the headline SQuAD 2.0 result quoted in the abstract. It exceeds every non-BERT row and is the endpoint of the +5.1 claim.
The F1 improvement claimed over the previous best system, computed as 83.1 minus 78.0 on the test split. It is a single-model result achieved without TriviaQA augmentation.
The date of the leaderboard snapshot in the first block. The scores are a moving target, so the paper fixes a date rather than claiming a standing rank.

items.caption: Table 4: SWAG Dev and Test accuracies. †Human per- formance is measured with 100 samples, as reported in the SWAG paper.
items.title: The SWAG Commonsense Scoreboard
items.takeaway: On SWAG's four-way sentence-completion task, BERT_LARGE reaches 86.3% test accuracy, which the paper reports as +27.1 points over the dataset authors' own ESIM+ELMo baseline and +8.3 points over OpenAI GPT. That figure also sits above the 85.0 scored by a single human expert, though the dagger footnote says the human numbers come from only 100 samples, so the human comparison rests on much thinner ground than the model comparisons.
items.walkthrough:
This is a seven-row scoreboard for a single task: [[swag-dataset]], the Situations With Adversarial Generations set of 113k sentence-pair completion examples. Each example gives one sentence and four candidate continuations, and a system must pick the most plausible one. The paper calls this [[grounded-commonsense-inference]] — everyday plausibility rather than logical entailment.

The metric in both number columns is plain accuracy: the percentage of examples where the chosen continuation was the correct one. With four choices, guessing at random would land near 25.

**The two columns.** *Dev* is the development split, the [[dev-set-model-selection]] half used for tuning; *Test* is the withheld split. A dash means that system's authors never reported that split, not that it scored zero. BERT_BASE has a dev number and no test number; OpenAI GPT has the reverse.

**Reading the blocks.** Three horizontal rules split the rows into prior systems, BERT, and human ceilings.

The first block is what existed before. ESIM is a BiLSTM sentence-pair inference model, and the two rows differ only in the word representations fed into it: static GloVe vectors, which give every occurrence of a word the same vector, versus [[elmo]], which reads the sentence and produces context-sensitive ones. Swapping in ELMo moves test accuracy from 52.7 to 59.2. Then [[openai-gpt]], a fine-tuned left-to-right Transformer, jumps to 78.0.

The second block is this paper's [[bert-base-and-bert-large]]. Fine-tuning packs the context with each candidate into its own sequence; one learned vector is dotted with each sequence's [[cls-token]] vector, and a softmax over the four scores picks a winner. That is the only new parameter added.

**What it shows.** Take the test column. $86.3 - 59.2 = 27.1$, the gain over ESIM+ELMo. And $86.3 - 78.0 = 8.3$, the gain over GPT.

The last block is the ceiling. A single expert scores 85.0, so BERT_LARGE is 1.3 above it; five annotations combined score 88.0, still 1.7 ahead of BERT. The dagger warns these came from 100 samples in the SWAG paper, a sample small enough that a couple of points either way means little.

terms.definition: Situations With Adversarial Generations, a dataset of 113k sentence-pair completion examples testing everyday plausibility judgements. It is the only task this table reports.
The first column, naming the model or human baseline whose accuracy the row reports. Rows are grouped by horizontal rules into prior work, BERT, and human ceilings.
The development split of SWAG, the held-out portion used for tuning hyperparameters and picking checkpoints. Numbers here are self-reported and not leaderboard-verified.
The withheld evaluation split of SWAG, used for the final comparison between systems. Both of the paper's headline gains are computed from this column.

The implicit metric in both number columns: the percentage of examples where the system picked the correct one of the four candidate continuations. It is not labelled in the table because the caption names it.
Marks a cell where that split was never reported for that system, rather than a score of zero. It appears for OpenAI GPT on Dev, BERT_BASE on Test, and both human rows on Dev.

The Enhanced Sequential Inference Model, a BiLSTM-based architecture built for sentence-pair inference. Here it is the hand-designed task architecture that the SWAG authors used for their own baselines.
Static pre-trained word vectors, where each word type gets one fixed vector regardless of the sentence it appears in. It is the weaker of the two representations fed into ESIM.
The ESIM architecture with static GloVe word vectors as input, the weakest system in the table. It sets the floor the other rows are read against.

A feature-based model that runs separately trained left-to-right and right-to-left LSTM language models over the sentence and concatenates their states into context-sensitive word features. The underlying model stays frozen; only the task architecture on top is trained.

The same ESIM architecture with ELMo's contextual features instead of GloVe vectors, and the baseline the SWAG dataset's own authors reported. The paper treats this as the reference point for its +27.1 claim.

A fine-tuning approach that pre-trains a left-to-right Transformer language model and then fine-tunes all of its weights on the target task. It is the strongest prior system in the table and the closest architectural comparison to BERT.
The smaller BERT configuration, sized to match OpenAI GPT's parameter count so the comparison isolates bidirectionality rather than model capacity. Only its Dev score is reported here.
The larger BERT configuration and the paper's headline system on this task, shown in bold in both columns. Every comparison the accompanying text draws uses this row.

Marks the best model score in each column, both belonging to BERT_LARGE. The human rows are not bolded even though 88.0 is numerically higher, because they are a ceiling rather than a competing system.
The accuracy of one expert annotator answering SWAG questions, taken from the SWAG paper. It is the single-person ceiling BERT_LARGE is said to pass.
The accuracy obtained by combining five human annotations per example, which averages away individual mistakes. It is the higher ceiling that BERT_LARGE does not reach.
The footnote marker on both human rows. It records that human performance was measured on only 100 samples and is quoted from the SWAG paper, not re-measured here.

The final hidden vector at the special first position of each packed sequence, used as the aggregate representation of that whole context-plus-candidate pair. On SWAG a single learned vector is dotted with it to produce that candidate's score.
The kind of judgement SWAG asks for: which continuation of a described situation is plausible in the everyday world. It differs from entailment, where the answer follows logically from the premise.

numbers.meaning: The number of sentence-pair completion examples in SWAG. It is stated in the section text, not in the table, and is large enough that the paper's note about small datasets being hyperparameter-sensitive does not apply here.
The number of candidate continuations per SWAG example. It sets the shape of the fine-tuning head: four packed sequences, four scores, one softmax.
Chance accuracy, derived rather than printed: with four choices, random guessing is right one time in four. Every number in the table should be read as a distance above this floor.
ESIM+GloVe Dev and Test accuracy. Static word vectors plus a hand-built inference architecture land barely twice chance, which is the point of SWAG being called adversarial.
ESIM+ELMo Dev and Test accuracy, and the SWAG authors' own baseline. Replacing GloVe with ELMo's contextual features adds about 6.5 points over the GloVe row.
OpenAI GPT's Test accuracy; its Dev score is not reported. Fine-tuning a pre-trained left-to-right Transformer adds roughly 19 points over the best feature-based system.
BERT_BASE's Dev accuracy; no Test number was reported for it. Since BERT_BASE is sized to match GPT, the gap over GPT is attributed to bidirectional pre-training rather than to extra capacity.
BERT_LARGE's Dev accuracy, bolded as the best on that split. It is 5.0 points above BERT_BASE's 81.6, the table's only within-BERT size comparison.

BERT_LARGE's Test accuracy, bolded, and the number both headline comparisons are computed from. It is 0.3 below its own Dev score, the small drop expected when moving from a tuned split to a withheld one.
The gain the paper claims over the ESIM+ELMo baseline, from 86.3 minus 59.2 on Test. It is a difference of 27.1 accuracy points, not a 27.1% relative increase, despite the percent sign.
The gain over OpenAI GPT, from 86.3 minus 78.0 on Test. Again these are accuracy points; the paper writes it without a plus sign in the running text.
A single human expert's accuracy, quoted from the SWAG paper. BERT_LARGE's 86.3 sits 1.3 points above it, which is the basis for saying BERT passes the single expert.
Accuracy when five human annotations per example are combined, quoted from the SWAG paper. BERT_LARGE remains 1.7 points below this, so the aggregate human ceiling is not reached.

The number of samples the human accuracies were measured on, per the dagger footnote. At that size a single point of accuracy is one example, so 85.0 and 88.0 carry much wider uncertainty than the model scores.
The number of human annotations combined in the last row. Pooling several annotators averages away individual slips, which is why 88.0 exceeds the single expert's 85.0.
The fine-tuning settings the paper used to produce the BERT rows. They are drawn from the same small grid used for the other tasks, so nothing task-specific was added beyond the one scoring vector.

items.caption: Table 5: Ablation over the pre-training tasks using the BERTBASE architecture. “No NSP” is trained without the next sentence prediction task. “LTR & No NSP” is trained as a left-to-right LM without the next sentence prediction, like OpenAI GPT. “+ BiLSTM” adds a ran- domly initialized BiLSTM on top of the “LTR + No NSP” model during fine-tuning.
items.title: Pre-training Task Ablation
items.takeaway: Holding architecture, data and fine-tuning fixed, the table charges each drop in score to one removed piece of the pre-training recipe. Dropping next sentence prediction costs a little; replacing the masked LM with a left-to-right LM costs much more, above all on SQuAD (88.5 to 77.8 F1), and bolting a BiLSTM onto the left-to-right model repairs only part of that gap while making the GLUE numbers slightly worse.
items.walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

Four models, one per row, each pre-trained from scratch and then fine-tuned on five tasks. Every row uses the [[bert-base-and-bert-large|BERT_BASE]] architecture, the same [[pre-training-data|pre-training corpus]], the same hyperparameters and the same fine-tuning scheme. Only the pre-training objective changes.

That is what makes this an [[ablation-studies|ablation]]. One ingredient is removed at a time, so a drop down a column can be charged to the thing that was removed.

### How to read it

The five columns are scores on the [[dev-set-model-selection|development split]], not the withheld test split. Four are [[glue-benchmark|GLUE]] tasks scored by accuracy: [[mnli|MNLI-m]] (three-way entailment, matched genres), [[qnli|QNLI]] (does this sentence contain the answer?), [[mrpc|MRPC]] (are these two sentences paraphrases?) and [[sst-2|SST-2]] (sentiment). The fifth is [[squad-v1-1|SQuAD]] v1.1, scored by [[f1-score|F1]] on token overlap between the predicted [[answer-span]] and the gold one. Higher is better in every column.

### The rows

BERT_BASE trains on both pre-training tasks: the [[masked-language-model|masked LM]] and [[next-sentence-prediction|next sentence prediction]] (NSP).

[[no-nsp-ablation|No NSP]] keeps the masked LM and deletes NSP.

[[ltr-no-nsp-ablation|LTR & No NSP]] also has no NSP, and swaps the masked LM for a standard [[left-to-right-language-model|left-to-right]] LM. The left-only constraint is kept at fine-tuning too, since lifting it created a [[pretrain-finetune-mismatch|pre-train/fine-tune mismatch]]. The paper calls this row directly comparable to [[openai-gpt|OpenAI GPT]].

[[bilstm-on-top-of-ltr|+ BiLSTM]] is that same left-to-right model with a randomly initialised [[bilstm|BiLSTM]] stacked on top at fine-tuning, as a good-faith attempt to feed right-side context back in.

### What it shows

Compare row 1 with row 2 to isolate NSP. QNLI falls 88.4 to 84.9, a drop of 3.5. MNLI falls 0.5 and SQuAD 0.6. The paper calls all three drops significant; only the QNLI one is large, so read that claim with the sizes in front of you.

Compare row 2 with row 3 to isolate direction, since neither has NSP. MRPC falls 86.5 to 77.5 and SQuAD 87.9 to 77.8. The paper's reason for SQuAD: a left-to-right token's hidden state has no right-side context, and span prediction needs it.

Row 4 recovers SQuAD to 84.9, still 3.6 below BERT_BASE, and nudges every GLUE column down.

terms.definition: The stub heading over the first column, which lists model variants rather than tasks; the tasks are the column headings to its right.

The spanning header saying all five numbers come from each dataset's development split, the split used for tuning and model selection, not the held-out test split whose labels GLUE does not distribute.

Multi-Genre Natural Language Inference, matched section: given a premise and a hypothesis, label the pair entailment, contradiction or neutral. 'Matched' means the dev examples come from the same genres as training.
Question NLI, a recasting of SQuAD as binary classification: does this sentence contain the answer to this question? Negatives are sentences from the same paragraph that do not.

Microsoft Research Paraphrase Corpus: sentence pairs pulled automatically from online news and human-labelled for whether the two sentences mean the same thing. It is small, around 3,600 training examples.
Stanford Sentiment Treebank, binary version: label a single sentence from a movie review as positive or negative.
Stanford Question Answering Dataset v1.1: given a question and a Wikipedia passage that contains the answer, mark the span of the passage that answers it.
Accuracy, the fraction of dev examples classified correctly, expressed as a percentage. It is the metric for the four GLUE columns.

The harmonic mean of precision and recall over tokens, giving partial credit when the predicted span overlaps the gold span without matching it exactly. SQuAD's other metric, exact match, is not shown here.

The smaller of the paper's two configurations, 12 layers, hidden size 768, 12 attention heads, 110M parameters. Here it is the intact reference model, pre-trained on both masked LM and next sentence prediction, and the architecture every other row also uses.
A row: a model pre-trained with the masked LM but with the next-sentence-prediction task deleted. It is still bidirectional, so it isolates what NSP alone contributes.
BERT's second pre-training task: a binary decision, read off the [CLS] vector, about whether span B genuinely followed span A in the corpus or was sampled at random from elsewhere.
BERT's first pre-training task, kept in rows 1 and 2 and removed in rows 3 and 4: mask 15% of input tokens and predict each original from context on both sides.

A row: no next sentence prediction, and the masked LM replaced by a standard left-to-right language model. The left-only constraint is also applied at fine-tuning, because lifting it hurt downstream scores.
Left-to-right. Each token is predicted from the tokens before it only, so its hidden state never sees anything to its right.
Language model. Here, the standard next-token-prediction objective that the LTR row uses in place of the masked LM.
A row, indented because it modifies the row above rather than standing alone: the LTR & No NSP model with an extra recurrent layer added on top at fine-tuning time.

A bidirectional LSTM: an LSTM run forwards and another run backwards over the sequence, with the two directions' outputs joined at each position. It supplies right-side context that the LTR model's own layers lack.
The added BiLSTM starts from random weights and is trained only on the downstream task's labelled data, so unlike the layers below it, it gains nothing from pre-training.

The prior fine-tuning approach that pre-trains a left-to-right Transformer LM. The caption names it as the thing the LTR & No NSP row stands in for, though this row uses BERT's larger corpus, input representation and fine-tuning scheme.

The second stage: initialise from the pre-trained weights, attach a small task-specific output layer, and train everything end to end on the task's labelled data. All twenty cells are post-fine-tuning scores.
The caption's alternative spelling of the LTR & No NSP row label; it refers to the same model, the one the BiLSTM is stacked on.
An experiment that removes one component at a time from an otherwise fixed system, so any change in score can be attributed to what was taken away.

numbers.meaning: BERT_BASE, MNLI-m dev accuracy. The reference point for the entailment column; the paper gives no per-cell explanation, only the comparison to the rows below.
BERT_BASE, QNLI dev accuracy. The highest QNLI number in the table, and the one that falls most when NSP is removed.
BERT_BASE, MRPC dev accuracy. MRPC has only about 3,600 labelled training examples, so scores on it move more than on the larger sets.
BERT_BASE, SST-2 dev accuracy. The best in a column that barely moves across all four rows, spanning only 1.1 points.
BERT_BASE, SQuAD v1.1 dev F1. The reference span-prediction score, and the number the left-to-right rows fall furthest from.
No NSP, MNLI-m accuracy: 0.5 below BERT_BASE. The paper lists MNLI among the tasks where removing NSP hurts significantly, though this particular drop is under a point.
No NSP, QNLI accuracy: 3.5 below BERT_BASE's 88.4. The largest single cost attributed to dropping NSP anywhere in the table.
No NSP, MRPC accuracy: 0.2 below BERT_BASE, and the baseline against which the left-to-right row's MRPC collapse is measured.
No NSP, SST-2 accuracy: 0.1 below BERT_BASE, essentially unchanged. Single-sentence sentiment does not appear to need the sentence-pair objective.
No NSP, SQuAD F1: 0.6 below BERT_BASE. Named by the paper as one of the three tasks NSP removal hurts, and the fair comparison point for the LTR row since both lack NSP.
LTR & No NSP, MNLI-m accuracy: 1.8 below No NSP, the cost of giving up context from the right at every layer.
LTR & No NSP, QNLI accuracy: 0.6 below No NSP. QNLI loses far more to the NSP removal than to the loss of bidirectionality.
LTR & No NSP, MRPC accuracy: 9.0 below No NSP's 86.5, one of the two drops the paper calls large. The paper does not decompose why paraphrase detection suffers this much.
LTR & No NSP, SST-2 accuracy: 0.5 below No NSP. Sentiment is the one column where the left-to-right model stays close to the full model.
LTR & No NSP, SQuAD F1: 10.1 below No NSP and 10.7 below BERT_BASE. The paper's stated reason is that a left-to-right token's hidden state carries no right-side context, which span prediction needs.
+ BiLSTM, MNLI-m accuracy: identical to the row above, so the added recurrent layer changes nothing on this task.
+ BiLSTM, QNLI accuracy: 0.2 below the LTR row, a small loss rather than a gain.
+ BiLSTM, MRPC accuracy: 1.8 below the LTR row and the lowest cell in the table. It is the clearest instance of the paper's remark that the BiLSTM hurts the GLUE tasks.
+ BiLSTM, SST-2 accuracy: 0.5 below the LTR row and the lowest SST-2 figure shown.

+ BiLSTM, SQuAD F1: 7.1 above the LTR row's 77.8, which the paper calls a significant improvement, but still 3.6 below BERT_BASE's 88.5, so the randomly initialised recurrent layer only partly substitutes for bidirectional pre-training.
MRPC's approximate number of labelled training examples, stated in Section 5.2. It is context for why the MRPC column swings by eleven points across the table while SST-2 moves by one.
The share of input tokens the masked LM hides and predicts. It defines the objective present in rows 1 and 2 and absent in rows 3 and 4, and is fixed across all of them.

items.caption: Table 6: Ablation over BERT model size. #L = the number of layers; #H = hidden size; #A = number of at- tention heads. “LM (ppl)” is the masked LM perplexity of held-out training data.
items.title: The Model-Size Ladder
items.takeaway: Six separately pre-trained BERT models, from 3 layers up to 24, are lined up smallest to largest: held-out masked-LM perplexity falls at every step (5.84 to 3.23) while accuracy on MNLI-m, MRPC and SST-2 rises at every step. The paper reads this as evidence that scaling keeps paying off past sizes already considered large, and — its actual point — that the gains reach a task as small as MRPC, which has only 3,600 training examples.
items.walkthrough:
Each of the six rows is a separately pre-trained [[bert]] model. The three columns on the left, grouped under **Hyperparams**, say how that model was built. The four on the right say how it scored.

The build columns are the paper's size shorthand, [[model-size-notation]]. $\#L$ is the number of stacked [[transformer-encoder]] blocks. $\#H$ is the [[hidden-size-h]], the width of the vector passed between layers. $\#A$ is the number of [[self-attention]] heads inside each block.

Two quantities follow from those without being printed. Each head works in a subspace of size $H/A$, so $768/12$ gives 64 dimensions per head. And the feed-forward inner layer is [[feed-forward-filter-size]], $4H$ — 3072 when $H=768$.

**LM (ppl)** is [[masked-language-model]] perplexity on held-out training text: the exponential of the average cross-entropy the model pays on the tokens it was asked to fill in. Lower is better. It scores the pre-training objective itself, not any end task.

The last three columns are accuracy on [[glue-benchmark]] tasks, measured on the development split ([[dev-set-model-selection]]) after fine-tuning. [[mnli]]-m is matched-genre entailment, [[mrpc]] is paraphrase detection, [[sst-2]] is binary sentiment. Each cell is the mean over five [[fine-tuning-random-restarts]].

Now walk down. The smallest model, 3/768/12, sits at 5.84 perplexity and 77.9 / 79.8 / 88.4. The bottom row, 24/1024/16, sits at 3.23 and 86.6 / 87.8 / 93.7. Nothing in between reverses: perplexity falls at every step and all three accuracies rise at every step.

End to end that is $+8.7$ on MNLI-m, $+8.0$ on MRPC, $+5.3$ on SST-2.

Row two is a control on heads rather than depth. Holding 6 layers and $H=768$ fixed, cutting heads from 12 to 3 costs 0.56 perplexity and 1.3 MNLI points, so head count moves the result on its own.

Row four, 12/768/12, is BERT_BASE and row six is BERT_LARGE ([[bert-base-and-bert-large]]) — 110M and 340M parameters.

The claim ([[effect-of-model-size]]) is not that perplexity improves with size; the paper says that was already known. It is that MRPC improves too, despite its 3,600 examples and its distance from the pre-training tasks. Earlier [[feature-based-approach]] work found scaling stopped helping ([[prior-scaling-evidence]]); the authors hypothesise the difference is that [[fine-tuning-approach]] adds almost no freshly initialised weights ([[few-random-parameters-hypothesis]]).

Read the evidence as narrow. Three tasks, one averaged number per cell, no spread reported — and the prose says "all four datasets" where the table shows three accuracies plus perplexity.

terms.definition: The header spanning the three left-hand columns, meaning the architectural settings chosen before pre-training rather than anything measured. Everything else about training — data, optimiser, step count — was held identical across the six rows.

The header spanning the four right-hand columns, meaning results measured on each task's development split rather than its test split. Dev is the split the authors were free to evaluate on repeatedly, so these numbers are not directly comparable to the leaderboard test numbers elsewhere in the paper.
The number of Transformer encoder blocks stacked on top of each other in this model. Depth: how many rounds of self-attention plus feed-forward a token representation passes through.
The hidden size, meaning the dimension of the vector that represents each token between layers. Width: it also fixes the feed-forward inner size at 4H and the size of every attention projection.

The number of self-attention heads per block. The H dimensions are split across the A heads, so each head attends in an H/A-dimensional subspace and the heads' outputs are concatenated back to width H.

Perplexity of the masked language modelling objective, evaluated on held-out training data. It measures how well the pre-trained model fills in tokens it was asked to predict, before any fine-tuning happens.

The exponential of the average cross-entropy per predicted token, readable as an effective branching factor — roughly how many equally likely candidates the model is still hesitating between. Lower is better; because BERT predicts masked positions using context from both sides, these values are not comparable to a left-to-right language model's perplexity.

Text drawn from the same pre-training corpus but kept out of the pre-training updates, used here only to score the masked-LM objective. It measures fit to the pre-training distribution, not generalisation to any downstream task.

The matched section of Multi-Genre Natural Language Inference: given a premise and a hypothesis, label the pair entailment, contradiction or neutral. "Matched" means the dev examples come from the same genres as the training examples; it is the largest of the three tasks shown.

Microsoft Research Paraphrase Corpus: sentence pairs pulled automatically from online news, annotated for whether the two sentences mean the same thing. It is the small-data case in this table, and the one the section's argument turns on.
Stanford Sentiment Treebank, binary version: classify a single sentence from a movie review as positive or negative. A single-sentence task, unlike the two pair tasks beside it.
In the caption, the practice of varying one facet of the system at a time while holding everything else fixed, to see what that facet contributes. Here the varied facet is model size.

The caption's name for what is being varied: the joint setting of layers, hidden size and heads. The table does not report a parameter count per row, so "size" here is expressed only through L, H and A.

BERT's pre-training task, in which about 15% of input token positions are corrupted and the model must recover the original token from surrounding context on both sides. The LM (ppl) column scores exactly this task.
The paper's two headline configurations, which appear in this table as row four (12/768/12) and row six (24/1024/16). They are the only two rows whose parameter counts the surrounding text gives.

The step between the left block and the right block of this table: the pre-trained model is given a small task-specific output layer and all of its parameters are trained further on the task's labelled data. Each accuracy cell is a separately fine-tuned model.

Repeating fine-tuning from the same pre-trained checkpoint with different data shuffling and different classifier-layer initialisation. The paper reports the average over five of these per cell, because fine-tuning on small datasets was sometimes unstable.

The benchmark collection the three accuracy tasks are drawn from, which bundles several sentence and sentence-pair understanding datasets under one format. Only a selected three of its tasks appear here.

numbers.meaning: The #L column: layer counts for the six models, read top to bottom. They are chosen as a rough doubling ladder (3, 6, 12, 24) with 6 appearing twice so that the head-count comparison in row two can be made at fixed depth.

The #H column: hidden size. The first four models keep BERT_BASE's width of 768 while depth changes; the last two widen to BERT_LARGE's 1024, so depth and width are not varied independently across the whole table.
The #A column: attention heads. Head count tracks hidden size at 64 dimensions per head (768/12, 1024/16) in every row except row two, where 3 heads at H=768 gives 256 dimensions per head.

The LM (ppl) column: masked-LM perplexity on held-out training text, falling monotonically as the model grows. The paper offers no per-row explanation; it presents the whole column as a restatement of the already-known fact that larger models fit language modelling better.
The MNLI-m column: dev accuracy on three-way entailment, averaged over five fine-tuning restarts. Every step up in size raises it; a random-guess baseline on three balanced labels would be near 33.

The MRPC column: dev accuracy on binary paraphrase detection. This is the column carrying the section's argument, since MRPC has the least training data and still improves at every step, including the +0.2 from row four to row five and the +0.9 from row five to row six.

The SST-2 column: dev accuracy on binary sentiment. It rises monotonically too, but with the smallest total span of the three tasks, consistent with a single-sentence task where even the 3-layer model is already near 88.
