Accuracy gained from the smallest row to the largest on MNLI-m, MRPC and SST-2 respectively: 86.6 − 77.9, 87.8 − 79.8, 93.7 − 88.4. These are the spans the paper's claim about continued gains rests on.

The full perplexity drop across the table, a fall of 2.61, leaving the largest model at about 55% of the smallest model's perplexity. It confirms the pre-training objective itself keeps improving with size.

The cost of going from 12 heads to 3 heads at fixed 6 layers and H=768: perplexity worsens from 4.68 to 5.24, and MNLI-m falls from 81.9 to 80.6. This is the table's only controlled comparison of a single hyperparameter.

The number of random fine-tuning restarts averaged into each accuracy cell. The paper reports the mean only; no standard deviation or range is given, so cell-to-cell gaps of a few tenths cannot be checked against run-to-run noise.

MRPC's labelled training examples, quoted in the section text. It is the number that makes MRPC's monotone improvement the point of the table, since the concern was that a very large pre-trained model would have nothing extra to give a task this small.

Total parameters for BERT_BASE (row four, 12/768/12) and BERT_LARGE (row six, 24/1024/16). Roughly a threefold increase in parameters buys 2.2 MNLI points, 1.1 MRPC points and 0.8 SST-2 points in this table.

The largest Transformer in Vaswani et al. (2017), cited as the size the field had already reached, with 100M parameters in the encoder. The paper uses it to argue that its own gains occur on top of models already considered large.
The largest Transformer the authors say they found in the literature, from Al-Rfou et al. (2018). Deeper but narrower than BERT_LARGE, and still smaller in total parameters.
The bi-LM size increase in Peters et al. (2018b) that produced mixed downstream results. It is one of the two prior findings this table is arguing against.

The hidden dimensions in Melamud et al. (2016): going from 200 to 600 helped, and going further to 1,000 did not. The other prior finding this table argues against, and both prior works used a feature-based rather than fine-tuning setup.
The feed-forward inner width, always four times the hidden size. It is not a column in the table but it is implied by #H, so rows with H=768 use 3072 and rows with H=1024 use 4096.

Dimensions per attention head, also implied rather than printed. Five of the six rows sit at 64; row two's 3 heads at H=768 gives 256, an unusually wide head, and that row also has the worst perplexity for its depth.

The share of token positions selected for prediction in masked LM pre-training, which is what the LM (ppl) column is computed over. Perplexity here is therefore an average over masked positions only, not over every token in the held-out text.

The number of datasets the section text says improve strictly, against three accuracy columns plus the perplexity column actually shown. The discrepancy is in the paper; whichever reading is intended, the monotone pattern in the printed columns is what the evidence amounts to.

items.caption: Table 7: CoNLL-2003 Named Entity Recognition re- sults. Hyperparameters were selected using the Dev set. The reported Dev and Test scores are averaged over 5 random restarts using those hyperparameters.
items.title: Fine-tuned versus frozen BERT on NER
items.takeaway: On CoNLL-2003 named entity recognition, BERT scores close to the best published systems when fine-tuned, and — the point of the table — nearly as well when its weights are frozen and only its activations are fed to a small task model. Concatenating the top four hidden layers gives 96.1 Dev F1 against 96.4 for fine-tuning the same model, a gap of 0.3.
items.walkthrough:
Every number here is an [[f1-score|F1]] score on [[conll-2003-ner|CoNLL-2003]], the shared-task dataset used as the standard [[named-entity-recognition|named entity recognition]] benchmark. The task is [[token-level-tasks|per-token]]: tag each word with whether it names a person, an organisation, a location, and so on.

Two score columns. Dev F1 is the [[dev-set-model-selection|development split]], which the caption says was used to pick hyperparameters. Test F1 is the held-out split. A dash means that number was never reported, not that it was zero.

The rows fall into three blocks.

The top block is other people's published systems. [[elmo|ELMo]] scores 95.7 dev / 92.2 test and is the [[feature-based-approach|feature-based]] system BERT is arguing with. CVT reports test only, 92.6; CSE reports 93.1, printed bold as the best Test F1 anywhere in the table.

The middle block is BERT [[fine-tuning-approach|fine-tuned]] end to end, every pre-trained weight updated on the NER data. [[bert-base-and-bert-large|BERT_LARGE]] reaches 96.6 / 92.8 and BERT_BASE 96.4 / 92.4. Note that 92.8 is still 0.3 below CSE's 93.1, so the paper's word is "competitively with [[state-of-the-art|state-of-the-art]] methods", not "better than".

The bottom block is the experiment the section exists for. BERT_BASE is frozen; its activations are read out and fed to a [[frozen-feature-bilstm-classifier|randomly initialised two-layer 768-dimensional BiLSTM]] below the classifier, and no BERT parameter moves. Each row names [[layer-selection-ablation|which layer or layers]] the activations are taken from. Only Dev is reported for these.

Read down it. The input embedding layer alone, with no self-attention above it, gives 91.0. Any single hidden layer does much better — 94.9 for the top one, 95.6 for the one below it. Combining layers does better still: a weighted sum of the top four gives 95.9, and [[concat-last-four-layers|concatenating]] them gives 96.1. Weighting all twelve layers gives 95.5, below both top-four options, so more layers is not automatically better.

Now subtract. 96.4 minus 96.1 is 0.3.

The best frozen read-out lands within 0.3 Dev F1 of fine-tuning the same model. That is what the [[feature-based-approach-with-bert|section]] is built to show: BERT works as a fixed feature extractor, not only as something you fine-tune. The evidence is one task and Dev only, so it is a narrower claim than the eleven-task sweep elsewhere in the paper.

terms.definition: The left-hand column header, naming the model or model variant that produced each row's scores. Rows are a mix of other authors' published systems and this paper's own configurations.
F1 measured on CoNLL-2003's development split. The caption says hyperparameters were chosen on this split, so it is the tuning split rather than a clean held-out score.
F1 measured on CoNLL-2003's held-out test split, the number normally quoted for comparison against other papers.
The harmonic mean of precision and recall over predicted entity spans; the standard scoring metric for this benchmark. Higher is better, and it is reported on a 0-100 scale here.
The shared-task dataset from Tjong Kim Sang and De Meulder (2003), the standard NER benchmark of the time. The paper uses it as the testbed for comparing frozen features against fine-tuning.

Labeling each token with whether it belongs to a name — of a person, organisation, location and so on — and which type. It is a token-level task, so the model must produce an output at every position.
Marks a score that is not available: CVT and CSE did not publish Dev numbers, and the feature-based rows were not run on Test. It does not mean a bad score.

A published feature-based model that concatenates the representations of a separately trained left-to-right and a right-to-left language model, then feeds them into a task-specific architecture. It is the closest prior comparison for the frozen-feature setting.
Cross-View Training, a semi-supervised sequence modeling method from a contemporaneous paper. It appears here only as a published NER baseline; the paper does not describe how it works.
Contextual String Embeddings for sequence labeling, another published baseline. Its 93.1 Test F1 is bold as the best test score in the table, which BERT does not beat.

The block header for the setting used everywhere else in the paper: a classification layer is added on top of pre-trained BERT and all parameters, pre-trained ones included, are trained further on the NER data.
The larger pre-trained configuration, 24 Transformer layers with hidden size 1024 and 16 attention heads, about 340M parameters. Reported here only in the fine-tuned block.

The smaller configuration, 12 layers with hidden size 768 and 12 attention heads, about 110M parameters. It is the model used for every feature-based row, so its fine-tuned score is the fair comparison for them.

The block header for the ablation: BERT_BASE is kept frozen, activations are extracted from one or more of its layers, and those fixed vectors are the input to a separately trained task model. No BERT parameter is updated.

A recurrent layer run left-to-right and right-to-left over the sentence, its two directions joined at each position. Here it is randomly initialised, two layers deep, 768-dimensional, and sits between the frozen BERT features and the token classifier.
Features taken from BERT's input embedding layer, below any self-attention block. A token's vector therefore does not depend on the rest of the sentence beyond its position and segment.
Features taken from the output of layer 11 of BERT_BASE's 12 Transformer layers — the one just below the top.
Features taken from the output of the top Transformer layer, layer 12, the same vectors a fine-tuned model's classifier reads.
Each token's vectors from layers 9 through 12 are combined into one 768-dimensional vector by a weighted sum. The table does not state how the weights are set.

Each token's vectors from layers 9 through 12 are joined end to end into one longer vector, keeping all four layers' information rather than averaging it away. This is the best-scoring feature-based variant.
A weighted sum over the outputs of all twelve Transformer layers of BERT_BASE, from the lowest to the top. It scores below the top-four variants.
The vectors a Transformer layer outputs at each token position, which is what "extracting features" means here. In BERT_BASE each such vector is 768 numbers wide.
The settings not learned by gradient descent — learning rate, batch size, number of epochs. The caption says these were selected on the Dev set, which is why Dev is the tuning split.
Repeated training runs from the same starting checkpoint that differ only in random seed. Both reported columns are averages over 5 such runs, so a cell is a mean rather than a single run's score.
The typographic marking of the best Test F1 in the table, which belongs to CSE rather than to any BERT row.

numbers.meaning: ELMo's Dev and Test F1. The published feature-based baseline the paper wants to improve on; both BERT sizes beat it on both splits.
CVT's Test F1. Reported without a Dev number, so the dash in its Dev cell is missing data.
CSE's Test F1, printed bold as the highest Test F1 in the table. No BERT row here matches it.
Fine-tuned BERT_LARGE. Its Test F1 is 0.3 below CSE's 93.1, which is why the text says BERT_LARGE performs 'competitively with state-of-the-art methods' rather than claiming a new best.
Fine-tuned BERT_BASE. This 96.4 is the reference point for the whole bottom block, because every feature-based row freezes this same BERT_BASE model.
Dev F1 using only the input embedding layer's output. It is the lowest score in the table, since these vectors carry no information about the rest of the sentence.
Dev F1 from the second-to-last hidden layer, the best of the single-layer choices.
Dev F1 from the last hidden layer, 0.7 below the layer just beneath it. The top layer is not automatically the most useful one to read out.
Dev F1 from a weighted sum of the top four hidden layers — better than any single layer, but below concatenating the same four.
Dev F1 from concatenating the top four hidden layers, the best feature-based result in the table and the row the section's conclusion rests on.
Dev F1 from a weighted sum of all twelve layers. It is worse than both top-four variants, so mixing in the lower layers does not help here.

96.4 minus 96.1: how far the best frozen read-out sits behind fine-tuning the same BERT_BASE. The paper cites this gap as evidence that BERT is effective as a feature extractor as well. The same 0.3 separately describes BERT_LARGE's 92.8 from CSE's 93.1 on Test.
96.1 minus 91.0: how much the frozen model gains from reading contextual layers instead of the raw embedding layer.
The number of random restarts each reported score is averaged over, per the caption, using the hyperparameters chosen on Dev.
The number of Transformer layers in BERT_BASE, which fixes what 'all 12 layers' means and makes 'second-to-last' layer 11.
The number of top layers combined in the two 'last four' rows — layers 9 through 12 of BERT_BASE.
BERT_BASE's hidden size, so each layer emits a 768-number vector per token; also the stated width of the BiLSTM placed on top of the frozen features.
The depth of the randomly initialised BiLSTM that consumes the frozen features before the classification layer.
4 x 768: the width of a token's feature vector in the 'Concat Last Four Hidden' row, four times wider than in the weighted-sum rows. The paper does not report this number; it follows from the setup.
The year of the CoNLL shared task that defines this dataset and its Dev/Test splits.
Approximate parameter counts of BERT_BASE and BERT_LARGE, from the paper's model description rather than the table. They are why BERT_LARGE outscores BERT_BASE on both splits here.

items.caption: Figure 3: Differences in pre-training model architectures. BERT uses a bidirectional Transformer. OpenAI GPT uses a left-to-right Transformer. ELMo uses the concatenation of independently trained left-to-right and right-to- left LSTMs to generate features for downstream tasks. Among the three, only BERT representations are jointly conditioned on both left and right context in all layers. In addition to the architecture differences, BERT and OpenAI GPT are fine-tuning approaches, while ELMo is a feature-based approach.
items.title: BERT, GPT and ELMo Side by Side
items.takeaway: The figure states the paper's central architectural claim as arrows: only BERT lets every position depend on both its left and its right neighbours at every layer, GPT's arrows run one way, and ELMo's two one-way stacks meet only at the very top. The caption adds a second and separate difference: BERT and GPT adapt to a task by fine-tuning the whole model, while ELMo hands its outputs over as fixed features.
items.walkthrough:
Three boxes sit side by side, one per pre-training model: [[bert]], [[openai-gpt]] and [[elmo]]. Each box is the same schematic of one model reading one sequence of $N$ tokens. Nothing in it is a measurement — it is a drawing of connectivity.

### How to read one box

Read bottom to top. The yellow rectangles along the bottom, $E_1$ to $E_N$, are the input vectors, one per token position ([[input-embedding-sum]]). The green rectangles along the top, $T_1$ to $T_N$, are the vector each position ends up with ([[final-hidden-vector-ti]]), and those are what a later task consumes. The blue ellipses between them are the encoder units at each position and layer: `Trm` for a Transformer block ([[transformer-encoder]]), `Lstm` for an LSTM cell ([[lstm]]).

The arrows carry the argument. An arrow into a unit means that unit's value is allowed to depend on where the arrow came from.

### What the three boxes show

In BERT's box the arrows cross in both directions, at both drawn layers. Every position feeds every position in the layer above it, so a token's vector is shaped by words on both sides from the first layer onward. That is [[bidirectional-self-attention]], and the paper's name for the result is [[deep-bidirectionality]].

In GPT's box the arrows only ever travel up and to the right. Position 2 can see position 1; position 1 cannot see position 2. That is [[constrained-self-attention]], the shape a [[left-to-right-language-model]] objective forces on the encoder.

ELMo's box holds two dashed enclosures, each a stack of LSTMs over the same $E$'s. Arrows inside the left stack point right; arrows inside the right stack point left, giving a [[right-to-left-language-model]]. The two stacks never exchange anything, and the only place they meet is the arrows converging on each $T$ at the top, where their outputs are concatenated. The paper calls this [[shallow-concatenation]], as opposed to joint conditioning inside every layer.

### The second axis

The caption names a difference the drawing does not show: the two [[transfer-strategies]]. BERT and GPT are a [[fine-tuning-approach]]; ELMo is a [[feature-based-approach]], its $T$'s frozen and fed into a separate [[task-specific-architecture]].

terms.definition: The label on the left panel, marking it as this paper's model; "Ours" flags the authors' own system against the two baselines beside it. It is drawn as a stack of Transformer blocks in which every position connects to every position at every layer.

The middle panel: a Transformer language model pre-trained left-to-right, which the paper treats as the closest existing method to BERT. It is drawn with the same units as BERT so that the only visible difference is the direction of the arrows.
The right panel: a model that reads the sequence with a separate left-to-right and right-to-left LSTM stack and joins their outputs per token. It is the paper's example of a feature-based method.

A blue ellipse standing for one Transformer block acting at one position in one layer. Inside it are self-attention over the sequence and a position-wise feed-forward network, neither of which the figure draws.

A blue ellipse standing for one LSTM cell at one position in one layer of ELMo. Each cell passes state horizontally to its neighbour, which is why ELMo's within-stack arrows are horizontal while BERT's and GPT's cross diagonally.

The yellow rectangles along the bottom of every panel: the input vector for each token position, before any encoding. In BERT these are the sum of a token, segment and position embedding; the figure just treats them as "what goes in".

The green rectangles along the top of every panel: the final vector produced for each token position, which is what a downstream task reads. In ELMo's panel each $T$ is a concatenation of a left-to-right and a right-to-left vector rather than the output of a single stack.

The number of token positions in the input sequence, used only to name the last position; the figure shows positions 1, 2 and $N$ and elides the rest. It is not a fixed value for any of the three models.
The real content of the figure: an arrow from unit A to unit B means B's value may depend on A. Which arrows are absent is what separates the three panels.
Arrows running both up-left and up-right, so each unit receives from positions on both sides. This is the picture of self-attention with no directional mask.
Arrows that only travel up and to the right, so a unit receives from its own position and positions to its left. This is self-attention masked to left context only.

Each dashed rectangle groups one complete directional LSTM stack, left-to-right on the left and right-to-left on the right. The boundary marks that the two stacks are trained independently and exchange nothing while running.
The horizontal dots in each row indicating the omitted middle positions between token 2 and token $N$. It is a drawing convenience, not a model component.
The caption's description of BERT: a Transformer encoder whose attention is unmasked, so representations at every layer are formed from context on both sides.
The caption's description of GPT: the same encoder with attention masked so each token sees only what precedes it. This is what a standard language modeling objective permits.
The caption's phrase for ELMo's two stacks: each is trained as its own language model, one forward and one backward, with no shared computation. Neither ever conditions on the other's state.
Joining the forward and backward vector for a token end-to-end into one longer vector, which happens once, at the top. The paper calls this shallow because no layer below sees both directions.

terms.term: Jointly conditioned on both left and right context in all layers
terms.definition: The caption's claim for BERT alone: a representation is computed from both sides at once, at every depth, rather than assembled from two one-sided computations. It is the property the paper argues the two pre-training tasks buy.
Adapting to a task by adding a small output layer and continuing to train all pre-trained weights on the task's labeled data. The caption places BERT and GPT here.
Keeping the pre-trained model fixed and feeding its output vectors into a separately designed task model as extra input features. The caption places ELMo here.

The caption's description of what ELMo's $T$ vectors are for: inputs to a task-specific architecture, not a model to be trained further. This is the transfer-strategy difference, separate from the architecture difference.
The architecture used while learning from unlabeled text, before any task data is seen. The figure compares only this stage, which is where the directional constraints bite.
Yellow for inputs, blue for encoder units, green for outputs, held constant across all three panels. It lets the reader compare panels by shape and arrow pattern alone.

numbers.meaning: The figure's number in the paper; it appears in the appendix section that compares BERT, ELMo and GPT point by point. Also, coincidentally, the number of panels.

One box per model compared: BERT, OpenAI GPT, ELMo. The paper picks these three because they are the pre-training methods it positions itself against — one fine-tuning baseline and one feature-based baseline.

Token positions in the input sequence, running from the first to the last. Only the first two and the last are drawn, with dots for the rest, so the pattern of arrows is readable without crowding the box.

numbers.value: 2 (rows of Trm in the BERT and GPT panels)
numbers.meaning: The number of encoder layers drawn. Two is the smallest depth at which "at every layer" is visible — one layer would not show that the crossing pattern repeats — so the count is schematic, not the real depth.
The paper's real configurations are $L=12$ for BERT_BASE and $L=24$ for BERT_LARGE, far more than the two rows shown. The figure abbreviates depth because its subject is connectivity, not size.

One left-to-right stack and one right-to-left stack, drawn inside separate dashed enclosures. Two is not a stylistic choice here: it is the model, since ELMo's bidirectionality is exactly these two independent directional language models.

numbers.value: 2 (rows of Lstm inside each ELMo stack)
numbers.meaning: Each directional stack is drawn as two layers deep, matching the depth drawn for BERT and GPT so the panels stay comparable. The figure does not commit to this being ELMo's true depth.
The caption separates architecture — who can see whom — from transfer strategy — fine-tuning versus feature-based. They are independent: BERT and GPT differ on the first axis and agree on the second.

The two directional stacks are joined at exactly one place, the top, where their per-token outputs are concatenated into each $T$. The paper's word for this is "shallow", and Section 5.1 argues it is strictly less expressive than conditioning on both sides at every layer.

items.caption: Figure 4: Illustrations of Fine-tuning BERT on Different Tasks.
items.title: Four task shapes, one encoder
items.takeaway: Four families of downstream task are drawn as four copies of the same diagram, differing only in what is packed into the input sequence and which output vectors an arrow is attached to. The paper uses this to show that adapting BERT to a task means plugging in task-specific inputs and one extra output layer, not redesigning the model.
items.walkthrough:
Figure 4 draws the same model four times, once per family of task. Nothing inside the blue slab changes between the panels. Everything that differs sits at the edges: what is fed in at the bottom, and which vectors have an arrow leaving the top.

### Reading one panel

Work bottom to top.

The pink row is the input token sequence, after [[wordpiece-tokenization]] has split the text into subword units. Grey arrows carry each token up to the yellow row, the input embeddings $E$.

The blue slab is [[bert]] itself, a stack of [[transformer-encoder]] blocks. The faint circles and criss-crossing lines inside sketch [[bidirectional-self-attention]]: every position reads every other position.

The green row on top is what comes out — one final hidden vector per input position. $C$ sits above the [[cls-token]]; $T_i$ sits above token $i$. These are the [[contextual-representations]].

The red arrow is the only new part. It marks where a freshly initialised [[task-specific-output-layer]] is attached, and what that layer emits.

### The four panels

(a) Two texts are packed into one sequence, split by the [[sep-token]] and tagged by [[segment-embeddings]]. Braces under the pink row label them Sentence 1 and Sentence 2; primes mark the second text's positions. One red arrow leaves $C$ and emits a class label. Seven datasets are listed, from [[mnli]] through [[swag-dataset]].

(b) The same, with one text and no separator drawn mid-sequence. The label again comes off $C$ — this is the [[c-vector-classification-head]]. Datasets: [[sst-2]] and [[cola]].

(c) [[question-answering]] on [[squad-v1-1]]. Question and paragraph are packed as in (a), but the arrows now leave the paragraph's outputs $T'_1 \dots T'_M$, not $C$. Each paragraph token is scored twice, once as a span start and once as an end, by the [[span-prediction-head]].

(d) [[conll-2003-ner]]. Every $T_i$ gets its own arrow and its own label: O, B-PER, O.

### What it shows

Panels (a) and (b) are [[sentence-level-tasks]], reading from one vector. Panels (c) and (d) are [[token-level-tasks]], reading from many.

The claim is narrow but concrete. Across all four, only the red arrow is new; [[fine-tuning-bert]] then trains the whole stack end-to-end.

terms.definition: The pre-trained encoder, drawn as one opaque block because it is identical in all four panels. Its internal weights start from the same pre-trained checkpoint every time.
What the whole figure illustrates: initialising from the pre-trained weights, attaching the red output layer, and training every parameter on the task's labeled data.

The special token placed first in every input sequence, shown as the leftmost pink box in all four panels. It carries no word content; it exists to give the model a slot whose output can summarise the whole sequence.
The special token that closes one packed text and starts the next, drawn as the middle pink box in panels (a) and (c). It is the visible boundary marker between the two segments.
The WordPiece tokens of the first (or only) text, as pink boxes. Not necessarily whole words — rare words are split into pieces.
The tokens of the second packed text in panels (a) and (c). The prime is only bookkeeping: it says this position belongs to segment B, not segment A.
The input embedding of a token, before any Transformer layer runs. Each is the sum of a token embedding, a segment embedding and a position embedding.
The input embeddings of the two special tokens. They are ordinary learned vectors like any other token's, not a separate mechanism.
The final hidden vector sitting above [CLS] after the full encoder stack. In panels (a) and (b) it is the input to the classifier; in (c) and (d) it is computed but nothing is read from it.
The final hidden vector for input token i — the paper's contextual representation of that token, since self-attention has mixed in the rest of the sequence.
The final hidden vector above the separator token. It exists in panels (a) and (c) and is not read by any output head there.
The final hidden vectors of the second segment. In panel (c) these are the paragraph's token outputs, and they are exactly the vectors the span head reads.
The task-specific output layer added on top of BERT, and the only thing that changes across the four panels. Its weights are the ones learned from scratch.
The path from a discrete token to its input embedding, drawn once per position. They carry no learned task-specific parameters.

terms.term: Circles and criss-crossing lines inside the slab
terms.definition: A schematic of the encoder's layers, where each line suggests one position attending to another. The picture is deliberately not to scale with the real 12 or 24 layers.
Labels marking which tokens belong to which packed text. In this paper a 'sentence' means any contiguous span of text, not a grammatical sentence.
The label in panels (b) and (d), where only one text is fed in. The paper describes this as a degenerate text-∅ pair — the second slot is simply empty.
The output of panels (a) and (b): one discrete label for the entire input, produced from C by a single linear layer plus softmax.
The two texts packed into the SQuAD input. The question takes the A segment embedding and the paragraph takes B, so the model can tell which is which.
The output of panel (c): two distributions over paragraph token positions, one saying where the answer begins and one where it ends.
A named-entity tag meaning 'outside any entity'. Most tokens in a sentence get this tag, which is why it appears twice in panel (d).
A named-entity tag meaning 'beginning of a person name'. It is one entry from the CoNLL tag set; the figure shows it as a stand-in for the rest.

The family where two texts go in and one label comes out. The paper's argument here is that self-attention over the concatenation already performs the cross-attention that purpose-built pair models add explicitly.
One text in, one label out. Architecturally identical to (a) with an empty second segment.
A token-level task: the model marks a span of the input rather than emitting a label from a fixed set.
A token-level task where every position gets its own label from the same small tag set.
Multi-Genre Natural Language Inference: given two sentences, say whether the second is entailed by, contradicts, or is neutral toward the first.
Quora Question Pairs: decide whether two questions asked on Quora mean the same thing.
Question Natural Language Inference: SQuAD recast as a pair task — does this sentence contain the answer to this question?
Semantic Textual Similarity Benchmark: sentence pairs annotated with a graded similarity score rather than a discrete class. The B stands for Benchmark.
Microsoft Research Paraphrase Corpus: news sentence pairs labeled for whether they are semantically equivalent.
Recognizing Textual Entailment: a binary entailment task like MNLI, but with far less training data.

Situations With Adversarial Generations: pick the most plausible continuation of a sentence from four candidates. It is listed under (a) because each candidate is packed as sentence B and scored from C.
Stanford Sentiment Treebank: binary sentiment classification of single sentences taken from movie reviews.
Corpus of Linguistic Acceptability: binary classification of whether a single English sentence is linguistically acceptable.
Stanford Question Answering Dataset: crowdsourced question/answer pairs where the answer is always a span of a supplied Wikipedia passage.
The standard named entity recognition benchmark, from the 2003 CoNLL shared task. The paper formulates it as plain tagging, with no CRF layer on top.
The paper's split of the four panels: (a) and (b) read one vector for the whole input, (c) and (d) read a vector per token.

numbers.meaning: The number of sub-panels. The paper groups its eleven evaluation tasks into these four input/output shapes, which is the point of drawing four rather than eleven diagrams.
The token count of the first (or only) text. It is left as a letter because sequence length varies per example; the architecture does not depend on it.
The token count of the second packed text. A separate letter from N because the two segments have independent lengths.
Position indices within the sequence, counted after [CLS]. Panel (b) and (d) show T_1 and T_2 explicitly to make clear that every position produces its own output vector.
The SQuAD version drawn in panel (c). In v1.1 every question is answerable from the passage, so a start/end span always exists — which is what lets the head be just two distributions over positions.
The binary version of the Stanford Sentiment Treebank: positive or negative, rather than the finer-grained label set.
The year of the CoNLL shared task whose NER dataset is used. It names the dataset, not a quantity.
The number of additional output layers added per task. The paper states this directly: task-specific models are BERT plus one output layer, so a minimal number of parameters is learned from scratch.
The number of classes for a classification task, and the number of rows of the new weight matrix W. It is 3 for MNLI and 2 for the binary GLUE tasks.
The shape of W, the only new parameters for panels (a) and (b). The loss is log(softmax(CW^T)) — an ordinary linear classifier on C.
The width of every green vector in the figure. It is set by the pre-trained configuration, not by the task, which is why the same head shape works everywhere.

The entire task-specific parameter budget for panel (c): a start vector S and an end vector E, each of dimension H. P_i = exp(S·T_i) / Σ_j exp(S·T_j) gives the start distribution, with the analogous formula for the end.
The score of a candidate answer span running from position i to position j. The prediction is the highest-scoring span subject to j ≥ i, which rules out spans that end before they start.
MNLI's label count — entailment, contradiction, neutral. It is the one task in panel (a) that is not binary.
The similarity range STS-B annotators used. It is graded rather than categorical, so STS-B sits slightly awkwardly under a panel labeled classification.

The number of candidate continuations per SWAG example. Each is packed with the context as its own sequence, so one example becomes four forward passes whose C-scores are softmaxed against each other.
The sizes of SQuAD v1.1 and SWAG respectively. Both are large enough that the paper reports fine-tuning being insensitive to hyperparameter choice, unlike small sets such as RTE.

numbers.value: batch 16 or 32; Adam learning rate 5e-5, 3e-5 or 2e-5; 2, 3 or 4 epochs
numbers.meaning: The fine-tuning grid the paper found workable across all four panels. Everything else is kept at the pre-training settings, and dropout stays at 0.1.

numbers.value: at most 1 hour on a single Cloud TPU
numbers.meaning: The cost of reproducing any result in the paper from the pre-trained checkpoint. It is the practical claim behind the figure: the expensive part happened once, before any of these four panels.

items.caption: Figure 5: Ablation over number of training steps. This shows the MNLI accuracy after fine-tuning, starting from model parameters that have been pre-trained for k steps. The x-axis is the value of k.
items.title: MLM vs. Left-to-Right Over a Million Steps
items.takeaway: Fine-tuning from progressively later pre-training checkpoints shows that MNLI accuracy is still climbing at 1,000,000 steps, so BERT's long pre-training run is not wasted. It also shows that the masked LM objective is behind a left-to-right objective at the very first checkpoints, overtakes it before 100k steps, and finishes roughly two points ahead.
items.walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

Two curves from the paper's [[ablation-studies]]. Each curve is one pre-training objective, and each plotted marker is a separate fine-tuning run.

The procedure behind a single marker goes like this. Pre-training is halted after $k$ steps and the weights are saved. Those saved weights are then [[fine-tuning-bert|fine-tuned]] on [[mnli]], a three-way entailment task over sentence pairs. The fine-tuned model is scored on MNLI's development split — the held-out set used for [[dev-set-model-selection|model selection]], not the hidden GLUE test set.

That accuracy is the marker's height.

### How to read the axes

The x-axis is $k$, pre-training steps in thousands, spanning about 20 to 1,000. Labelled ticks sit at 200, 400, 600, 800 and 1,000, and the scale is linear. So the three earliest checkpoints — roughly 20k, 50k and 100k — are crushed against the left edge, and the steepest climb of both curves happens inside that thin strip.

The y-axis is MNLI Dev accuracy in percent, gridded at 76, 78, 80, 82 and 84. The window is narrow, so a two-point difference fills a quarter of the plot height.

Blue triangles are [[bert-base-and-bert-large|BERT_BASE]] pre-trained with the [[masked-language-model|masked LM]]. Red crosses are the same BERT_BASE configuration pre-trained as a [[left-to-right-language-model]] instead.

### What it shows

Two claims, one per question the appendix asks.

First: more pre-training keeps paying. Both curves are still rising at the right edge, with no flat stretch. The text puts a figure on it — almost 1.0% more MNLI accuracy at 1M steps than at 500k. Note that 500k is not itself a plotted point; reading between the 400k and 600k triangles gives about 83.6, against about 84.4 at 1M.

Second: the two objectives cross. At the leftmost checkpoint the red curve is *above* the blue one, roughly 79.4 against 78.6. That is the [[mlm-convergence-cost|convergence cost]] of masking: only [[masking-rate-15-percent|15% of token positions]] produce a prediction loss per batch, so each masked-LM step carries less signal than a left-to-right step, which predicts at every position.

The blue curve catches up before 100k and never falls back. By 1,000k it reaches about 84.4 against about 82.2 — a gap of roughly 2.2 points.

The paper hedges the first half of that and not the second: MLM "does converge slightly slower," but "begins to outperform the LTR model almost immediately."

One gap in the figure itself: the legend says only "Left-to-Right." The comparable left-to-right run in Section 5.1 is [[ltr-no-nsp-ablation|LTR & No NSP]], trained without [[next-sentence-prediction]], but Figure 5 does not restate that.

terms.definition: The x-axis label. One step is one gradient update during pre-training on unlabeled text; the axis is measured in thousands of such updates, so "400" means 400,000 steps.

The caption's symbol for the number of pre-training steps completed before the checkpoint was saved. The x-axis is the value of $k$, and each point is a model fine-tuned from that $k$-step checkpoint.

The y-axis: percentage of MNLI development-set sentence pairs classified correctly after fine-tuning. Dev, not test, so these numbers were available to the authors during development and are not GLUE leaderboard submissions.

Multi-Genre Natural Language Inference: given a premise sentence and a hypothesis sentence, predict entailment, contradiction, or neutral. It is the largest GLUE task and the paper's standard probe for ablations.
Taking the pre-trained weights as initialization, adding a small output layer, and training every parameter on MNLI's labeled data. Every point on the plot is the end of one such run.
A snapshot of the pre-trained model parameters saved partway through pre-training. This figure exists because the authors kept snapshots at several values of $k$ rather than only the final one.
An experiment that varies or removes one facet of the method to see how much it contributes. Here the varied facet is how long pre-training ran, crossed with which pre-training objective was used.

The smaller of the paper's two configurations: 12 layers, hidden size 768, 12 attention heads, 110M parameters. Both curves use this configuration, so size is held fixed and only the objective differs.
BERT's pre-training task: mask a random subset of input tokens and predict the originals using context from both sides. It is the blue series.
A standard language modeling objective: predict each token from the tokens preceding it only. It is the red series, and stands in for the prior generation of pre-trained models such as OpenAI GPT.
The blue legend entry, drawn with open triangle markers and a blue line. It is BERT_BASE pre-trained normally.
The red legend entry, drawn with cross markers and a red line. It is BERT_BASE's architecture and data with the masked LM objective swapped for a left-to-right one.

Used here in the training sense: how quickly accuracy stops improving as steps accumulate. The question the figure answers is whether masking, by supervising fewer positions per batch, makes that approach slower.
The appendix phrasing for how much text one gradient step sees — 256 sequences of 512 tokens, so 128,000 tokens. It sets the scale of what a single x-axis unit costs.

numbers.meaning: The labelled y-axis gridlines, in percent MNLI Dev accuracy. The axis starts near 75 rather than 0, so the vertical spread exaggerates differences: the whole visible range is under ten accuracy points.
Labelled x-axis ticks, in thousands of pre-training steps. The spacing is linear and even, which is why the early checkpoints bunch up at the left.
The eight checkpoint positions where markers appear on each curve. The first three sit in the compressed left margin; the last five line up with the labelled ticks.
The full pre-training run, and the rightmost point on the x-axis. Appendix A.2 states it: batch size 256 sequences for 1M steps, roughly 40 epochs over the 3.3 billion word corpus, taking four days.
Tokens per pre-training batch — 256 sequences times 512 tokens. The appendix quotes "128,000 words/batch * 1,000,000 steps" as the compute the question is asking about.
Masked LM accuracy at the earliest checkpoint (about 20k steps), the lowest point on the plot. It is below the left-to-right curve at the same step count, which is the convergence-cost effect.
Left-to-right accuracy at the earliest checkpoint. Roughly 0.8 points above MLM, and the only clear region where red leads blue.
The two curves around 100k steps, essentially level. The crossover happens somewhere between the 50k and 100k checkpoints, which is what the paper means by MLM outperforming "almost immediately."
The first plotted point where the blue curve is visibly clear of red, by about 1.2 points.
Both curves are flattening, but blue is still gaining faster; the gap has widened to roughly 1.5 points.
The gap reaches about 2.1 points. From here the red curve is nearly flat while blue still creeps upward.
Near-final values. MLM has gained about 0.35 points over the previous 200k steps, LTR about 0.2.
The endpoints. Neither curve has gone flat, which is the visual support for the claim that the full run is worth its cost.
The final gap between the two objectives at 1M steps. The figure's evidence for bidirectional masked pre-training beating left-to-right pre-training under matched architecture, data and fine-tuning.

The appendix's stated MNLI gain from 1M steps over 500k steps, answering whether BERT really needs such a long pre-training run. Note 500k is not a plotted checkpoint; interpolating between the 400k and 600k triangles gives about 83.6, so 84.4 minus 83.6 is roughly 0.8 to 0.9 — consistent with "almost 1.0".
The comparison point the appendix names when quantifying the late-training gain. It appears in the text only, not as a marker on the plot.

The fraction of WordPiece token positions masked for prediction in each sequence. It is the reason MLM might be expected to converge slower: only 15% of positions produce a prediction loss per batch, against every position for a left-to-right LM.
The pre-training corpus size (BooksCorpus 800M plus English Wikipedia 2,500M) and how many passes 1M steps amounts to. Context for what the far right of the x-axis costs, from Appendix A.2.

items.caption: Table 8: Ablation over different masking strategies.
items.title: The masking mixture ablation
items.takeaway: Six BERT pre-training runs that differ only in what happens to a token once it has been selected for prediction. Changing the mixture barely moves the fine-tuned scores, but pre-training with [MASK] alone costs 0.9 F1 on NER when BERT is frozen and used as a feature extractor. That single column is the paper's evidence for keeping the 80/10/10 mixture rather than always inserting [MASK].
items.walkthrough:
Six rows, six pre-training runs. Each run differs from the others in one respect only: what actually happens to a token once it has been picked out for prediction.

[[masked-language-model|The masked LM objective]] picks [[masking-rate-15-percent|15% of the WordPiece positions]] in each sequence at random. A row's three percentages then split those picked positions three ways. [[mask-same-rnd-strategies|MASK]] substitutes the [[mask-token|[MASK] placeholder]], SAME leaves the token untouched, and RND substitutes a random token from the vocabulary. In all three cases the original token remains the prediction target.

So the top row, [[masking-recipe-80-10-10|80/10/10]], is the recipe BERT actually ships: of the 15% chosen, 12% of all tokens become [MASK], 1.5% stay as they are, and 1.5% become something random.

### The right-hand block

Three [[dev-set-model-selection|development-set]] scores per run. MNLI Fine-tune is accuracy on [[mnli|MNLI]]. The two NER columns are [[f1-score|F1]] on [[conll-2003-ner|CoNLL-2003]] [[named-entity-recognition|named entity recognition]], scored two ways.

NER Fine-tune trains every BERT parameter on the task, as in [[fine-tuning-approach|the fine-tuning approach]]. NER Feature-based freezes BERT and feeds [[concat-last-four-layers|the concatenated top four hidden layers]] into a separate classifier, as in [[feature-based-approach|the feature-based approach]].

That last column carries the argument. Mixing strategies exists to soften the [[pretrain-finetune-mismatch|pre-train/fine-tune mismatch]]: [MASK] is everywhere in pre-training and never appears afterwards. A frozen BERT [[feature-based-amplifies-mask-mismatch|cannot adjust its representations to that absence]], so the mismatch should surface here first.

The appendix does not state which model size these runs use, so read the rows against each other rather than against the paper's headline numbers.

### What the rows show

The MNLI column reads 84.2, 84.3, 84.1, 84.4, 83.7, 83.6. The four rows that use some [MASK] sit within 0.3 of each other. The two that use none are the bottom two. NER fine-tune behaves similarly, 94.8 to 95.4, a spread of 0.6.

The paper reads this as fine-tuning being "surprisingly robust" to the mixture.

The feature-based column separates one row. Pure masking, 100/0/0, scores 94.0, while every other row is 94.6 or higher and 80/10/10 reaches 94.9 — a 0.9 F1 gap in a column that otherwise varies by 0.3.

That one cell is the case for keeping SAME and RND. It is a single run with no variance reported, and no fine-tuned setting shows a comparable penalty.

terms.definition: The left block of the table. Its three columns give the probabilities, within a single pre-training run, of each of the three things that can be done to a token that has been selected for prediction.
The right block. Scores on the held-out development split of two downstream tasks, used here to compare runs rather than to report final test numbers.
The strategy of replacing the selected token with the special [MASK] symbol before the model sees the sequence. This is what "masking" normally means, and the column gives how often it is applied.

The strategy of leaving the selected token exactly as it is in the input, while still asking the model to predict it at that position. The model cannot tell from the input which unchanged tokens it will be scored on.

The strategy of replacing the selected token with a different token drawn at random from the vocabulary. The target is still the original token, so the model must correct a corruption rather than fill a blank.

The reserved placeholder symbol substituted for a token the model must predict. It exists only during pre-training and never appears in downstream task inputs, which is the whole reason this ablation exists.

BERT's pre-training task: select a random subset of input token positions and train the model to predict the original tokens there from context on both sides. Every row of this table is a run of that task with a different corruption mixture.
The token at a selected position whose original identity the model must predict. It stays the target under all three strategies, regardless of what the input shows at that position.
Multi-Genre Natural Language Inference, a large sentence-pair task with three labels (entailment, contradiction, neutral). Used here as the sentence-level probe; the score is Dev accuracy.
The column heading for MNLI Dev accuracy after fine-tuning all of BERT's parameters on MNLI. There is no feature-based MNLI variant in this table.

Named entity recognition on CoNLL-2003: label each token with whether it is part of a person, organisation, location or miscellaneous name. Used here as the token-level probe, scored by F1 on the Dev set.
NER Dev F1 when every BERT parameter is trained further on the NER data. The pre-trained weights can move, so the model can adapt to inputs that contain no [MASK].

NER Dev F1 when BERT is frozen and its activations are used as fixed input features to a separate classifier. Here the features are the concatenated top four hidden layers, feeding a randomly initialised two-layer 768-dimensional BiLSTM.
Appears twice, once under MNLI and once under NER. In both cases it means all pre-trained parameters were updated on the labeled task data.
An experiment that varies one facet of the method while holding everything else fixed, to see how much that facet contributes. Here the varied facet is the masking mixture.

Any systematic difference between the inputs a model sees during pre-training and those it sees later. The specific mismatch at issue is that [MASK] appears constantly in pre-training and never downstream.
The harmonic mean of precision and recall over predicted entity spans, the standard CoNLL-2003 metric and the unit of both NER columns.
The development (validation) split, held out from training but distinct from the test set. All six numbers in each column come from it, so they are comparison figures, not headline results.

numbers.meaning: The fraction of WordPiece positions in each sequence chosen at random for prediction. It is fixed across all six rows and is not shown in the table; the row percentages divide up this 15%, they do not change it.
Row 1, the mixture BERT actually uses: of the chosen positions, 80% get [MASK], 10% are left unchanged, 10% get a random token. It is the reference row that the other five are compared against.
Row 2: every chosen position becomes [MASK]. This is the naive version of masked LM, and the one where the pre-train/fine-tune mismatch is largest.
Row 3: the same 80% [MASK], with the remaining 20% all replaced by random tokens and nothing left unchanged. It isolates whether the SAME strategy is doing any work.
Row 4: the same 80% [MASK], with the remaining 20% all left unchanged and no random replacement. It isolates whether the RND strategy is doing any work.
Row 5: [MASK] is never used; a fifth of chosen positions are left as-is and four fifths are corrupted at random. The model still gets a prediction task, but never sees the placeholder symbol.

Row 6: every chosen position is replaced by a random token. Pre-training inputs now look like ordinary text with noise in them, which removes the mismatch entirely but also removes the clean 'something is missing here' signal.

Row 1 restated as a share of all tokens rather than of chosen tokens: 80%, 10% and 10% of the 15% selection rate. Useful because it shows the recipe corrupts only about 3% of tokens in ways other than masking.
MNLI Dev accuracy for the 80/10/10 recipe. It is the reference value for the MNLI column, and notably not the highest one.
MNLI Dev accuracy for 100/0/0. Pure masking is 0.1 above the shipped recipe here, which is why the paper does not argue for the mixture on fine-tuned MNLI grounds.
MNLI Dev accuracy for 80/0/20. The lowest of the four [MASK]-using rows, by 0.3.

MNLI Dev accuracy for 80/20/0, the highest cell in the column. Dropping RND entirely does not hurt MNLI, which is part of why the paper calls fine-tuning robust rather than claiming an MNLI win for 80/10/10.
MNLI Dev accuracy for 0/20/80. One of the two rows that never use [MASK], and 0.5 below the recipe.
MNLI Dev accuracy for 0/0/100, the lowest cell in the column, 0.6 below the recipe. The paper singles out RND-only as performing 'much worse'.
NER Dev F1, fine-tuned, for 80/10/10. The highest cell in that column.
NER Dev F1, fine-tuned, for 100/0/0. It sits 0.5 below the recipe, a real but small gap given that no variance is reported.
NER Dev F1, fine-tuned, for both 80/0/20 and 80/20/0. The two partial mixtures land on the same value, 0.2 under the full recipe.
NER Dev F1, fine-tuned, for 0/20/80 — the lowest cell in that column, 0.6 below the recipe.
NER Dev F1, fine-tuned, for 0/0/100. Removing [MASK] entirely costs only 0.5 F1 once BERT's weights are allowed to move.
Frozen-BERT NER Dev F1 for 80/10/10, the highest cell in the column and the value the paper's recommendation rests on.
Frozen-BERT NER Dev F1 for 100/0/0, the lowest number anywhere in the table's right block. This is the one cell that separates the pure-[MASK] run from every other run.

Frozen-BERT NER Dev F1 for 80/0/20, 0/20/80 and 0/0/100. Three quite different mixtures land on the same value, which is what makes the 94.0 look like a specific effect of masking-only rather than general noise.
Frozen-BERT NER Dev F1 for 80/20/0, the second-best cell in the column and 0.2 below the full recipe.
The F1 gap between 80/10/10 (94.9) and 100/0/0 (94.0) in the frozen feature-based column. It is the largest single effect in the table and the paper's main quantitative support for the mixture.
The range across the five feature-based cells once 100/0/0 is excluded: 94.6 to 94.9. It sets the scale against which the 0.9 gap is read as meaningful.
The full range of the MNLI column, 83.6 to 84.4. Small enough that the paper describes fine-tuning as robust to the masking strategy.
The range across the four rows that use some [MASK]: 84.1 to 84.4. Within this group the mixture makes almost no MNLI difference.
The range of the NER fine-tune column, 94.8 to 95.4. Again small, and again the basis for the robustness claim.
The number of top hidden layers concatenated to form the frozen features in the feature-based column. Section 5.3 found this the best of the layer choices tested.
The width and depth of the randomly initialised BiLSTM that sits on top of the frozen features before the tag classifier. It is the only trained component in the feature-based setting.

How far the best feature-based NER setup trailed full fine-tuning in the paper's earlier comparison. It gives the expected cost of freezing BERT with the standard recipe, before any masking mismatch is added on top.

items.caption: GLUE classification loss, log(softmax(CW^T)) (unnumbered, Sec. 4.1) - the only new parameters fine-tuning introduces
items.title: The GLUE Classification Head
items.takeaway: This inline expression is the whole task-specific model BERT adds for a GLUE sentence-classification task: take the final hidden vector at the [CLS] position, multiply it by one new weight matrix to get one score per label, and train with ordinary cross-entropy. The paper's point in printing it is how little there is — a single $K \times H$ matrix is the only parameter matrix fine-tuning introduces.
items.walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

One line of math from Section 4.1, printed inline rather than as a numbered equation. It is the entire task-specific part of BERT on the [[glue-benchmark]]. Everything else in the model was fixed during pre-training.

Two objects appear.

$C$ is the [[final-hidden-vector-c]] — the top-layer output at the position of the [[cls-token]], the special token that sits first in every input sequence. The paper calls it the *aggregate representation* of the input, whether that input is one sentence or a packed pair. It lives in $\mathbb{R}^{H}$, where $H$ is BERT's [[hidden-size-h]].

$W$ is the [[c-vector-classification-head]]: a matrix in $\mathbb{R}^{K \times H}$, with $K$ the number of labels the task has.

### How to read it

Work outward from the inside.

Treat $C$ as a single row of $H$ numbers, so $C$ is $1 \times H$. Transposing $W$ gives an $H \times K$ matrix. The product $CW^{T}$ is therefore $1 \times K$ — one raw score, or logit, per possible label. That is a dot product of $C$ against each of $W$'s $K$ rows, so each row of $W$ acts as a learned direction that the pooled vector is scored against.

$\mathrm{softmax}$ turns those $K$ scores into a probability distribution over the labels. The $\log$ puts it back on a log scale, and training maximizes the log-probability of the gold label — equivalently, minimizes its negative. The paper writes the whole thing compactly and just calls it "a standard classification loss."

No bias vector is printed. No hidden layer, no pooling network, no task-specific encoder.

### What it shows

The claim being made is about parameter count, not accuracy. Fine-tuning trains every weight in BERT [[end-to-end-fine-tuning]], but $W$ is the only weight matrix that did not exist before fine-tuning started. For a three-way task with $H = 1024$, that is $3 \times 1024 = 3{,}072$ new parameters against 340M pre-trained ones.

This is the [[minimal-task-specific-parameters]] goal made concrete: adapting to a new sentence-level task means choosing $K$ and initializing one matrix.

terms.definition: The final hidden vector at the [CLS] position, i.e. the top-layer output of the Transformer encoder for the first input token. The paper uses it as the aggregate representation of the entire input sequence.
The special classification token prepended to every input sequence. Its final hidden state is the vector $C$ that this loss reads; here it is the only position the classifier looks at.
The space $C$ lives in: a real vector of length $H$. It says the pooled representation is a single vector of the model's hidden width, not a sequence.
BERT's hidden size, the width of the vectors passed between layers. It fixes the length of $C$ and the number of columns of $W$.
The classification layer weights, the one new parameter matrix fine-tuning introduces for a GLUE task. Each of its $K$ rows is a learned direction scored against $C$.
The shape of $W$: $K$ rows of $H$ numbers each. One row per output label, each the same width as the pooled vector it multiplies.
The number of labels in the task being fine-tuned on. It is the only thing about this head that changes from one GLUE task to another.
The transpose of $W$, so an $H \times K$ matrix. Transposing is what makes the shapes line up for a row-vector $C$ on the left.
The matrix product of the $1 \times H$ pooled vector with the $H \times K$ transposed weights, giving $K$ raw scores. One score per candidate label, before any normalization.
One of the $K$ unnormalized scores produced by $CW^{T}$. Not printed in the equation, but the standard name for what softmax consumes.
The normalization applied to the $K$ logits, turning them into a probability distribution over the labels. Here it operates over the label axis, not over the vocabulary as in the Masked LM head.

The natural logarithm applied after softmax, putting the label probabilities on a log scale. Training maximizes the log-probability of the correct label, which is the negative of the usual cross-entropy loss.

The paper's own phrase for this objective, signalling that nothing unusual is going on: cross-entropy over $K$ labels. The compact notation $\log(\mathrm{softmax}(CW^{T}))$ leaves the selection of the gold label's entry implicit.

The paper's term for $C$: a single vector standing in for the whole input, whether that input is one sentence or a sentence pair. It is what makes a fixed-size classifier possible over variable-length text.

The General Language Understanding Evaluation benchmark, the collection of sentence and sentence-pair tasks this loss is used for. Section 4.1 applies the same head to every one of its classification tasks.

The second stage of BERT's framework: plug in task inputs and outputs, then train all parameters on labeled task data. This equation is the entire output side of that plugging-in for GLUE classification.
Weights that did not exist in the pre-trained checkpoint. The paper's claim is that for GLUE this set is exactly $W$, and nothing else.

numbers.meaning: The hidden size of BERT_BASE (L=12, A=12), so $C$ has 768 entries and $W$ has 768 columns when fine-tuning the base model. Set in Section 3 as the base configuration, chosen to match OpenAI GPT's model size for comparability.
The hidden size of BERT_LARGE (L=24, A=16), so $C$ has 1024 entries and $W$ has 1024 columns when fine-tuning the large model. The larger of the paper's two released configurations.
The row count of $W$. It is not a fixed number: it is whatever the task's label set size is, which is why the paper states it as a definition rather than a value.
The label count for MNLI, whose three classes are entailment, contradiction and neutral (Appendix B.1). The largest $K$ among the GLUE classification tasks the paper reports.
The label count for the binary GLUE tasks — QQP, QNLI, SST-2, CoLA, MRPC, RTE — each of which asks a yes/no question about one sentence or a pair. Most of the benchmark sits at this value.
The size of $W$ for a three-label task on BERT_LARGE, worked out from $K \times H$. Given here only to make the scale of the new head concrete; the paper does not print this arithmetic.
The total parameter count of BERT_BASE, from Section 3. It is the number the 'only new parameters' claim is implicitly measured against for the base model.
The total parameter count of BERT_LARGE, from Section 3 and Section 5.2. Against it, a $K \times H$ matrix of a few thousand weights is the whole task-specific addition.
The number of new parameter matrices fine-tuning introduces for GLUE, and the number of output layers added on top of the encoder. This count is the actual point of the sentence the equation closes.

items.caption: Start-of-span probability, P_i = exp(S.T_i) / sum_j exp(S.T_j) (unnumbered, Sec. 4.2) - softmax over paragraph tokens
items.title: The start-position softmax
items.takeaway: This is the whole task-specific output layer BERT adds for extractive question answering: one learned vector $S$ is dotted with each passage token's final hidden vector, and a softmax over those scores gives a probability distribution over where the answer span starts. A second vector $E$ does the same for the end, and training maximizes the summed log-likelihood of the correct start and end positions.
items.walkthrough:
You are looking at the output layer BERT attaches for extractive [[question-answering]]. It is one line of algebra that turns the encoder's per-token outputs into a probability distribution over where the answer begins.

Start with the pieces. The question and the passage are concatenated into a single input, the question tagged with the A segment embedding and the passage with the B segment embedding ([[packed-question-passage-sequence]]). Running that sequence through BERT produces one vector per token at the top layer. $T_i$ is the vector at position $i$ ([[final-hidden-vector-ti]]), and it has $H$ components, where $H$ is the model's [[hidden-size-h]].

Then the new parameter. Fine-tuning introduces a start vector $S \in \mathbb{R}^H$, learned from scratch on the labelled data ([[start-and-end-vectors]]). It is one vector, the same one applied at every position.

### How to read it

The numerator, $e^{S \cdot T_i}$, exponentiates a dot product. Both $S$ and $T_i$ are $H$ numbers long, so $S \cdot T_i$ multiplies them componentwise and adds the $H$ products, collapsing to a single scalar. Read that scalar as a raw score for "token $i$ starts the answer".

The denominator sums the same exponentiated score over $j$, with $j$ running over every token of the paragraph. Dividing by that sum makes the $P_i$ non-negative and makes them total one across positions.

So $P_i$ is the probability, given this question and passage, that the answer starts at token $i$ ([[answer-span]]).

### What it shows

The end of the span uses the identical formula with a second learned vector $E \in \mathbb{R}^H$ substituted for $S$. Nothing else in the expression changes.

The training objective is the sum of the log-likelihoods of the correct start position and the correct end position — two softmax cross-entropy terms, added.

The point the paper is making: the entire reading-comprehension head is two $H$-dimensional vectors ([[minimal-task-specific-parameters]]). Everything else that makes the prediction work already sits in the pre-trained encoder, which is updated end-to-end alongside them ([[fine-tuning-bert]]). Turning the two distributions into one predicted span is a separate decoding step ([[span-score-and-decoding]]).

terms.definition: The probability that the answer span starts at token $i$ of the paragraph. It is the quantity the formula defines, and the $P_i$ over all paragraph positions sum to one.
The start vector, a single learned $H$-dimensional vector introduced only at fine-tuning time. Its dot product with a token's final hidden vector scores that token as the beginning of the answer.

The end vector, the companion to $S$: another learned $H$-dimensional vector, used in an identical formula to produce the distribution over end positions. It does not appear in this equation but is defined in the same sentence of the paper.
The final hidden vector at position $i$ — the top-layer output BERT produces for that token, described in the paper as its contextual representation. Here $i$ indexes a token of the passage.
The same object as $T_i$ under a different index, used inside the denominator's sum. The letter $j$ is the running index over all paragraph tokens.
The candidate start position: the index of the paragraph token being scored. The paper says "word $i$", though the sequence is tokenized into WordPiece pieces.
The summation index in the denominator, ranging over every token of the paragraph. Elsewhere in the same paragraph $j$ also denotes the candidate end position of a span, a separate use.

The dot product of the start vector with token $i$'s final hidden vector: multiply the two $H$-long vectors componentwise and add the results, giving one scalar. That scalar is the unnormalized start score for token $i$.
Exponentiation of the dot-product score, applied in both numerator and denominator. It makes every score positive so the ratio behaves as a probability.
The sum over all paragraph tokens, forming the normalizing constant. Because it ranges over positions rather than a vocabulary, the resulting softmax is a distribution over places in the passage.

The space of real vectors of length $H$; the paper writes $S \in \mathbb{R}^H$ and $E \in \mathbb{R}^H$. It says these two vectors have the same width as the encoder's hidden states, which is what lets the dot product be taken.
BERT's hidden size, the width of the vectors passed between layers and therefore the length of each $T_i$. It is 768 for BERT_BASE and 1024 for BERT_LARGE.
The exponentiate-and-normalize operation this formula performs, taken over token positions in the passage. It converts the per-token start scores into a probability distribution over start positions.
The contiguous stretch of passage tokens that answers the question, identified by a start position and an end position. This equation supplies only the start half of that pair.
The Wikipedia text that contains the answer, packed after the question in the same input sequence using the B segment embedding. The softmax is normalized over its tokens, not over the question's.
The paper's name for the only two parameters added for SQuAD fine-tuning. Everything else in the task model is pre-trained encoder weights, updated end-to-end.

The training objective: the log of the predicted probability of the correct start position plus the log of the predicted probability of the correct end position, maximized. In practice that is two softmax cross-entropy terms added together.
The Stanford Question Answering Dataset, the task this head is built for: given a question and a Wikipedia passage known to contain the answer, mark the answer span.

numbers.meaning: The length of each final hidden vector $T_i$, and therefore the length of $S$ and $E$. It is fixed by the pre-trained model's architecture, not chosen for this task — the start and end vectors simply have to match it for the dot product to be defined.

The number of vectors introduced at fine-tuning: one start vector $S$ and one end vector $E$. The paper stresses this count — "we only introduce" these two — because minimal task-specific parameters is the design claim being made.

The total number of newly initialized scalar parameters in the span head, following from the two vectors of width $H$. Against a pre-trained encoder of 110M or 340M parameters, this is the sense in which the head is described as minimal.

The $P_i$ sum to one across paragraph positions, by construction of the denominator. That is what makes the output a distribution over start positions rather than a set of independent per-token scores.
The number of crowdsourced question/answer pairs in SQuAD v1.1, per the paper's opening sentence of Section 4.2. It is the labelled data on which $S$ and $E$ are learned.
How long SQuAD fine-tuning runs. The paper states it flatly as a setting; fine-tuning is cheap enough that short schedules suffice.
The learning rate used for SQuAD fine-tuning, the largest value in the paper's usual fine-tuning grid of 5e-5, 3e-5 and 2e-5.
The batch size for SQuAD fine-tuning, the same value used across the GLUE tasks.

The constraint applied at decoding time, not in this equation: the predicted end position must not precede the predicted start, so the chosen span is well-formed. It appears in the sentence immediately after the formula.

items.caption: Candidate span score, S.T_i + E.T_j, maximised over j >= i (unnumbered, Sec. 4.2)
items.title: The additive span score
items.takeaway: A candidate answer running from token $i$ to token $j$ is scored by adding its start score $S{\cdot}T_i$ to its end score $E{\cdot}T_j$, and the prediction is whichever pair with $j \geq i$ scores highest. The whole answer-selection machinery is two dot products and a comparison, with no module that looks at the span as a unit.
items.walkthrough:
This is the rule BERT uses to choose an answer on [[squad-v1-1]]. The paper writes it inline in Section 4.2, with no equation number.

Two pieces of notation come first. Fine-tuning for this task introduces exactly two new parameter vectors, a start vector $S$ and an end vector $E$, each of dimension $H$ ([[start-and-end-vectors]]). $T_i$ is the top-layer output at position $i$ ([[final-hidden-vector-ti]]), that token's representation after the encoder has read the whole question-plus-passage sequence.

### How to read it

Pick one candidate [[answer-span]]: the stretch of passage tokens running from $i$ to $j$. Score its start with the dot product $S{\cdot}T_i$. Score its end with $E{\cdot}T_j$. Add the two numbers. That sum is the span's score.

Nothing else enters. The start term never looks at $j$, and the end term never looks at $i$.

### Why addition

The paper defines a start distribution over the paragraph's words, $P_i = \frac{e^{S \cdot T_i}}{\sum_j e^{S \cdot T_j}}$, and says an analogous formula gives the end. Training then sums the log-likelihoods of the correct start position and the correct end position — two separate predictions, each with its own softmax.

So $S{\cdot}T_i$ and $E{\cdot}T_j$ are logits from two independent distributions. Adding logits corresponds to multiplying the two probabilities, because $\log(p_{\text{start}} \cdot p_{\text{end}})$ is $\log p_{\text{start}} + \log p_{\text{end}}$. The two softmax denominators are the same for every candidate span, so they do not change which span wins. Ranking spans by the raw sum is therefore the same as ranking them by the product of start and end probabilities.

### The constraint

$j \geq i$ keeps the span well-formed: the end may not fall before the start. Setting $j = i$ gives a one-token answer, which is allowed. Without the constraint, an unconstrained maximum could return a pair whose "end" precedes its "start" ([[span-score-and-decoding]]).

Prediction is then an argmax over all valid $(i, j)$ pairs — scan them, keep the best.

One consequence for the design: adapting the pre-trained encoder to extractive QA costs two vectors, not a purpose-built reading-comprehension architecture ([[span-prediction-head]]).

One limit worth naming. The score is an unnormalised sum of dot products, so it is comparable within one passage but not across passages. [[squad-v2-0]] has to reintroduce a calibrated threshold to decide when to abstain.

terms.definition: One of the two vectors added at fine-tuning time, of dimension $H$. Its dot product with a token's final hidden vector scores how well that token works as the first token of the answer.

The mirror of $S$: an $H$-dimensional vector whose dot product with a token's final hidden vector scores that token as the last token of the answer. Note that the paper also uses $E$ elsewhere for input embeddings; here it means the end vector.
The final hidden vector the encoder produces at position $i$, in $\mathbb{R}^H$. It is that token's contextual representation, computed with the question and the whole passage visible.
The same object at position $j$, the candidate end of the span. It is read by $E$ rather than by $S$.
The index of the candidate start token in the packed sequence. It ranges over the passage's tokens.
The index of the candidate end token. In the score it ranges over the passage; in the decoding rule it is restricted to positions at or after $i$.
The inner product of two $H$-dimensional vectors, collapsing them to a single real number. Here it turns a token representation into one start score or one end score.
The start score of token $i$: an unnormalised logit saying how strongly the model wants the answer to begin there.
The end score of token $j$, the analogous logit for the answer finishing there.
The well-formedness constraint on a span: the end position must be at or after the start position. Equality means a single-token answer.
Any contiguous run of passage tokens from some $i$ to some $j$, considered as a possible answer before scoring. Every such pair gets a score; only one is predicted.
The probability that word $i$ starts the answer span, obtained by softmaxing the start scores over all words in the paragraph. The paper says the analogous formula gives the end probability.
The paper's name (introduced in Section 4.3) for the score of the best non-null span, that is the maximum of $S{\cdot}T_i + E{\cdot}T_j$ over pairs with $j \geq i$.
The maximisation that turns the per-span score into a prediction: take the highest-scoring valid pair. The position of the maximum, not its value, is what gets returned as the answer.
The encoder's hidden size, so also the length of $S$, $E$ and every $T_i$. It fixes how many terms each dot product sums.
The single input BERT sees for this task: the question tagged with the A segment embedding, then the passage tagged with B. Span indices $i$ and $j$ point into this sequence.
In SQuAD v2.0 only, the score of answering nothing, computed as $S{\cdot}C + E{\cdot}C$ using the [CLS] vector in place of a real span. It gives the abstain option a score on the same scale.
In SQuAD v2.0 only, the margin by which $\hat{s}_{i,j}$ must beat $s_{null}$ before a non-null answer is predicted. It is chosen on the dev set to maximise F1.

numbers.meaning: The number of task-specific vectors introduced for SQuAD fine-tuning: $S$ and $E$. The paper says 'we only introduce a start vector and an end vector during fine-tuning', so the score has exactly two additive terms.
The dimension of $S$, $E$ and each $T_i$, set by the encoder's hidden size rather than by the QA task. It is the length of each dot product, so $S$ and $E$ together add 1,536 or 2,048 new parameters.
The decoding constraint. It admits spans of length $j - i + 1 \geq 1$ and rules out pairs whose end precedes their start, which the unconstrained maximum would otherwise be free to return.

The number of valid $(i, j)$ pairs the argmax ranges over for a passage of $n$ tokens: $n$ choices of start, and for a start at $i$ there are $n - i + 1$ ends. For a 150-token passage that is 150 x 151 / 2 = 11,325 candidates. The paper does not state this count; it follows from the rule.

The size of SQuAD v1.1, described as 100k crowd-sourced question/answer pairs from Rajpurkar et al. (2016). Each pair supplies one correct start position and one correct end position as the training signal for $S$ and $E$.
The SQuAD v1.1 fine-tuning settings stated immediately after this equation. They are the standard fine-tuning grid values the paper reports, not something derived from the scoring rule.
The corresponding settings for the SQuAD v2.0 model, which reuses this same score plus the $s_{null}$ comparison. TriviaQA data was not used for that model.

items.caption: SQuAD 2.0 null-answer rule, s_null = S.C + E.C versus best span score, predict non-null when s-hat_{i,j} > s_null + tau (unnumbered, Sec. 4.3)
items.title: The Null-Answer Threshold Rule
items.takeaway: This is the prediction-time rule BERT uses on SQuAD 2.0, where a question may have no answer. It scores "no answer" as an ordinary span that starts and ends at [CLS], compares it against the best real span, and only outputs a real span when that span wins by more than a constant tau, which is fitted on the dev set.
items.walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

Three lines that decide, at prediction time, whether the model answers or abstains on [[squad-v2-0]] — the version of the dataset where the passage may simply not contain an answer ([[unanswerable-questions]]). Nothing here is learned as a rule. It is a comparison between two numbers, plus one constant fitted afterwards.

### How to read it

The scoring machinery is carried over unchanged from SQuAD v1.1. Fine-tuning adds only [[start-and-end-vectors]] $S$ and $E$, each dotted with a token's final hidden vector ([[final-hidden-vector-ti]] $T_i$). A span running from token $i$ to token $j$ therefore scores $S{\cdot}T_i + E{\cdot}T_j$ ([[span-score-and-decoding]]).

The second line takes the maximum of that over all valid spans. The constraint $j \geq i$ keeps the end from landing before the start. Call that winner $\hat{s}_{i,j}$: the best real answer the model can find.

The first line does the same arithmetic with one substitution. The [[cls-token]] sits at position zero of every sequence, and its final vector is [[final-hidden-vector-c]] $C$. Putting $C$ in both slots scores a span that starts and ends at [CLS] ([[cls-as-null-span]]). That number, $s_{\texttt{null}}$ ([[null-span-score]]), is the model's score for "no answer exists here."

The third line compares them, offset by $\tau$.

### Why the offset

If $\tau$ were fixed at zero, the rule would just take whichever score is larger.
