But the two scores are not calibrated against each other — nothing in training forces the abstention score onto the same numeric scale as ordinary span scores. So [[tau-threshold]] sets how much better a real span must be before it beats abstaining. Raise $\tau$ and the model abstains more; lower it and it guesses more.

The paper picks $\tau$ on the [[dev-set-model-selection]] to maximize [[f1-score]], since on SQuAD 2.0 a correct abstention counts as a correct answer, so this trade-off has a measurable optimum.

### What it shows

Abstention is folded into the existing head as one extra position and one scalar. The paper calls this "a simple approach" and reports +5.1 F1 over the previous best system — a gain it attributes to the model, not to this rule. No ablation of $\tau$ is given, and no value for it is published.

terms.definition: The score of the no-answer span, computed as $S{\cdot}C + E{\cdot}C$. It is the model's numeric vote for abstaining on this question.
The score of the best real (non-null) span in the passage, i.e. the highest span score over all valid start/end pairs. This is the candidate that must beat abstention.
The start vector, one of only two task-specific parameter vectors introduced for SQuAD fine-tuning; its dot product with a token's final hidden vector scores that token as a span start.
The end vector, the counterpart to $S$; its dot product with a token's final hidden vector scores that token as a span end. Here it is the same $E$ used in SQuAD v1.1, reused unchanged.

The final hidden vector at the [CLS] position, the same $H$-dimensional output used elsewhere as the aggregate sequence representation. In this equation it stands in for both the start and the end token of the null span.
The final hidden vector produced by the top layer at passage position $i$ — that token's contextual representation. Dotted with $S$ it scores position $i$ as a span start.
The same kind of final hidden vector, at position $j$. Dotted with $E$ it scores position $j$ as a span end.
The index of the candidate answer span's start token within the packed question-plus-passage sequence.
The index of the candidate answer span's end token, required to be at or after $i$.
Maximization over all candidate spans whose end is not before their start. It selects the single best-scoring real span, which is what the rule then compares against abstention.

A scalar threshold added to the null score, setting how much better a real span must score before it is preferred over abstaining. It is chosen on the development set to maximize F1, not learned during fine-tuning.
The dot product between two $H$-dimensional vectors, producing the scalar score used throughout this head.

The special token placed first in every BERT input sequence. For SQuAD 2.0 its position is added to the start and end probability space, so it can be selected as the answer span when no answer exists.
The degenerate span that both starts and ends at [CLS], used to represent the hypothesis that the passage contains no answer to the question.
A prediction that names an actual span of passage text, as opposed to abstaining. The rule emits one only when the inequality holds.
The reading-comprehension dataset extended so that some questions have no short answer in the provided paragraph; the paper describes this as making the problem more realistic.
The held-out development split, used here to fit $\tau$ rather than to report final results. Fitting a threshold on dev keeps the test set untouched.

The span-overlap metric SQuAD reports, giving partial credit for token overlap between prediction and gold answer. On SQuAD 2.0 a correct abstention counts as a correct answer, so $\tau$ has a real optimum under this metric.

numbers.meaning: The constraint on the maximization: a span's end index must be at or after its start index. Without it the maximum could pick an end token preceding the start, which is not a span at all.

The paper states only that τ is selected on the dev set to maximize F1; it reports no numeric value and no sensitivity analysis for it, so a reader cannot reproduce the exact operating point from the paper alone.
Epochs of fine-tuning for the SQuAD 2.0 model, reported in the same passage. One fewer than the 3 epochs used for SQuAD v1.1.
The fine-tuning learning rate for this model, the top of the paper's usual fine-tuning grid (5e-5, 3e-5, 2e-5) and the same rate used for SQuAD v1.1.
The fine-tuning batch size for SQuAD 2.0, larger than the 32 used for v1.1. The paper gives no reason for the difference; fine-tuning hyperparameters are chosen by search on dev.
The F1 improvement over the previous best system on SQuAD 2.0, excluding entries that use BERT as a component. It is the headline result the whole SQuAD 2.0 setup, including this rule, produces.
